verseByVerse.quote: When the angels went away from them into heaven, the shepherds said to one another, 'Let us go over to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.' And they went with haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the baby lying in a manger.
verseByVerse.commentary: The shepherds respond immediately: let us go. They do not debate or deliberate. They go with haste — and they find exactly what the angel said. The word, when acted upon, leads them to exactly what it promised. The extraordinary thing about the shepherds is not their piety but their obedience. They hear the word; they act on it; they find what it pointed to. That is faith in its simplest and most complete form.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they saw it, they made known the saying that had been told them concerning this child. And all who heard it wondered at what the shepherds told them.
verseByVerse.commentary: The shepherds become the first evangelists — making known what has been told them about the child. The response is wonder: everyone who hears it is amazed. Luke does not record conversions or belief; he records wonder, which is the beginning of both. The shepherds are not commissioned to preach; they simply cannot stop telling people what happened. That is the natural response of those who have seen what they have seen.

verseByVerse.quote: But Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart. And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen, as it had been told them.
verseByVerse.commentary: Luke draws a quiet contrast: the crowd wonders, the shepherds praise, and Mary treasures and ponders. Treasured implies careful keeping, like someone storing something precious. Mary is doing theology — taking the pieces of what has happened and turning them over in her mind, looking for their connections and their depth. She does not have all the answers; she has all the material, and she is working with it. The scene has the shape of complete worship: word received, sign confirmed, proclamation made, praise offered.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–40 — Jesus Presented at the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The presentation of Jesus at the temple is the scene where the old covenant meets the new — where the long story of Israel's worship, sacrifice, and waiting encounters the one toward whom the whole system has been pointing. Joseph and Mary bring Jesus to Jerusalem for two reasons, both required by the Law: the purification of the mother forty days after the birth of a son (Leviticus 12:1–8), and the presentation of the firstborn to the LORD (Exodus 13:2, 12–15; Numbers 18:15–16). They bring the offering of the poor — two turtledoves or two young pigeons rather than a lamb and a pigeon — which tells us clearly that the family of Jesus was poor. The King of heaven and earth is raised in poverty.

Simeon is described in terms that belong to the faithful remnant of Israel — righteous, devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, the Holy Spirit resting upon him. The “consolation of Israel” (paraklēsis tou Israēl) is the language of Isaiah 40 (“Comfort, comfort my people”) — the promised end of exile, the return of God to his people, the redemption of Jerusalem. Simeon has been waiting his whole life for this. The Holy Spirit has promised him specifically that he will not die before he sees the Lord's Christ. And now, as the young couple with the offering of the poor come into the temple courts, the Spirit moves Simeon to go to them. He takes the child in his arms, and everything he has spent his life waiting for is in his hands.

Simeon's song — the Nunc Dimittis (“Now you dismiss”) — is perhaps the most moving passage in Luke's first two chapters. “Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation.” He can die now. He has seen everything he was promised. The salvation he holds in his arms is not merely for Israel; it is “a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel” — the fulfilment of the Servant Songs of Isaiah (42:6; 49:6), the universal scope of the gospel announced before it has begun. And then the shadow falls: the child is set for the falling and rising of many in Israel, a sign to be opposed, and a sword will pierce Mary's own soul. Joy and sorrow are not opposites in Luke's Gospel; they are twins, born of the same truth. The one who is the light of the world will be rejected. The one whose birth the angels celebrated will die on a cross. Simeon holds the baby and sees it all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Simeon's announcement that the child is “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (v. 32) is the fulfilment of Isaiah's Servant Songs and the theological basis for the entire Gentile mission of Acts. From the moment of the presentation, the Gospel of Luke contains within it the seed of the global church. The child in Simeon's arms is not merely the king of the Jews; he is the light of the world. This is why Luke, writing for a Gentile audience, is the Gospel that most fully develops the universal scope of the gospel — it is the theological trajectory established here, in the temple courts, by an old man who has been waiting his whole life to say what he now says.

Simeon's warning to Mary — “a sword will pierce through your own soul also” (v. 35) — has been understood in the tradition as a reference to Mary's presence at the crucifixion (John 19:25–27), where she will stand at the foot of the cross and watch her son die. The sword is the sword of grief, of the suffering that participation in the Son's mission inevitably involves. But the phrase “that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed” (v. 35b) suggests a broader theological purpose: the coming of Jesus will force a crisis of decision in every heart. He does not leave people neutral. He is “set for the falling and rising of many” — his presence divides, reveals, exposes what is in people. This is the crisis of the gospel in every generation.
verseByVerse.examples:
Simeon's “now you are letting your servant depart in peace” is the model of a death well prepared for — not the resignation of someone who has given up, but the completion of someone who has received what they came for. He has seen the salvation of God. He can go. The Christian who knows that their salvation is secured, who has seen Jesus — not with physical eyes but with the eyes of faith — who has held him in the arms of trust — that person can face death with the same peace that Simeon found. Not because death is nothing, but because what lies beyond it is the same Jesus they have known in life.

Anna, the eighty-four-year-old prophetess who “did not depart from the temple, worshipping with fasting and prayer night and day” (v. 37), is Luke's portrait of long faithfulness. She has been waiting her entire adult life — possibly more than sixty years of widowhood — for the redemption of Jerusalem. She does not give up. She does not grow cynical. She does not stop praying because the answer has not come. And when the answer comes, she is right there, in the temple, where she has always been. The reward of patient faithfulness is rarely glamorous; it is being in the right place when God acts.

verseByVerse.quote: And at the end of eight days, when he was circumcised, he was called Jesus... And when the time came for their purification according to the Law of Moses, they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord... to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the Law of the Lord, a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus enters the covenant through circumcision on the eighth day, receiving the name the angel gave before he was conceived. He is then brought to the temple for the purification rites required after birth (Lev. 12) and the presentation of the firstborn (Exod. 13:2). The offering of turtledoves — the provision for those who cannot afford a lamb (Lev. 12:8) — is a quiet note of the family's poverty. The Son of God enters the world not only as a human being but as a poor human being, subject from birth to the law He will one day fulfil.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon, and this man was righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him. And it had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ. And he came in the Spirit into the temple...
verseByVerse.commentary: Simeon belongs to the faithful remnant waiting for Israel's consolation — the comfort and restoration the prophets promised. The Holy Spirit has been at work in him: He revealed the promise, and now He moves Simeon into the temple at exactly the appointed moment. Providence arranges an encounter between an old man who has waited his whole life and a forty-day-old child whose parents have come to fulfil a legal requirement. Neither party is aware of what is about to happen.

verseByVerse.quote: ...he took him up in his arms and blessed God and said, 'Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation that you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The Nunc Dimittis: Simeon has seen a forty-day-old baby and calls it your salvation. He has held six weeks of human life in his arms and declares his own life complete. What he has waited for, he has received — not a conquering king on a throne, but an infant in a temple courtyard. A light for revelation to the Gentiles — the universality that runs through Luke's Gospel sounds here for the first time in the narrative. This salvation is not merely for Israel; it has been prepared in the presence of all peoples. Simeon, old representative of faithful Israel, announces the global scope of the gospel. He can die in peace.

verseByVerse.quote: And his father and his mother marvelled at what was said about him. And Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother, 'Behold, this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that is opposed — and a sword will pierce through your own soul also — so that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The second part of Simeon's word is a warning to Mary personally. Jesus will divide: appointed for the fall and rising of many, a sign that is opposed. He is not a figure who unites everyone on easy terms; he is a touchstone that reveals what is in people. The sword that will pierce Mary's soul is almost certainly the cross — the moment when the mother watches her son die. Simeon plants this knowledge when Jesus is forty days old. She will carry it for thirty-three years.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a prophetess, Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was advanced in years... She did not depart from the temple, worshipping with fasting and prayer night and day. And coming up at that very hour she began to give thanks to God and to speak of him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary: Anna is the second witness at the presentation — the law required two (Deut. 19:15). Eighty-four years old, a widow since her early twenties, she has spent her decades in the temple in prayer and fasting. Where Simeon received a private revelation, Anna is a public figure whose life has been a sustained act of waiting and worship. She arrives at exactly the right hour — Providence again — and immediately speaks of the child to all who are waiting for redemption. Her years of prayer prepared her for a single moment of proclamation. That is not a waste; it is the investment of a lifetime.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had performed everything according to the Law of the Lord, they returned into Galilee, to their own town of Nazareth. And the child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom. And the favour of God was upon him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The holy family returns to Nazareth in obedience to the law they have fulfilled. The summary of Jesus's early childhood — grew, became strong, filled with wisdom, favour of God upon him — compresses three decades into one verse. The growth is genuine: Jesus develops as a human child develops, in body and wisdom. The divine favour rests on him not as a reward for performance but as the expression of the Father's delight in his Son. The extraordinary childhood is described in the most ordinary terms — and that combination is itself part of the mystery of the incarnation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–52 — The Boy Jesus in the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The only story from Jesus's childhood in any of the four Gospels is this one — Jesus at twelve years old in the temple, sitting among the teachers, asking and answering questions that leave the learned astonished. Luke includes it not as a charming anecdote but as a theological statement: even before his public ministry begins, Jesus is defined by a relationship with the Father that supersedes every other claim on his life, including the entirely legitimate claim of his parents. The story is not about a precocious child showing off his knowledge. It is about the Son of God beginning to understand — or beginning to express — who he is and what he has come to do.

The setting is the Passover — the feast of Israel's redemption, the meal that commemorates the night when the LORD passed over the houses marked with blood and the firstborn of Israel were spared. Jesus is twelve years old, the age at which a Jewish boy began to take on personal responsibility for the commandments (the formal bar mitzvah ceremony developed later, but the principle of adult religious responsibility at thirteen was well established). He is, for the first time, fully participating in the Passover as a responsible member of the covenant community. The irony that Luke intends his reader to feel is deep: the Passover Lamb is celebrating Passover.

When Mary and Joseph discover Jesus missing from the caravan and return to find him in the temple, Mary's question is entirely natural: “Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in great distress.” Jesus's answer is the first words of Jesus recorded in Luke's Gospel — and they are a claim of identity: “Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?” The word “must” (dei) is one of Luke's most significant theological words — it marks divine necessity, the compulsion of God's redemptive plan. Jesus must be about his Father's business. Not might, not should — must. And the “Father” he refers to is not Joseph. He distinguishes, gently but unmistakably, between the father who has been searching for him and the Father whose house he is in.
verseByVerse.theology:
The word dei (“it is necessary,” “I must”) appears forty times in Luke-Acts and marks the divine necessity driving the story forward: the Son of Man must suffer (9:22); he must rise on the third day (24:7); the Scripture must be fulfilled (22:37). Here, at twelve years old, Jesus uses it for the first time. This is not a child defying his parents; this is the Son of God expressing the first law of his existence: he must be about his Father's business. The whole of Luke's two-volume work is the outworking of this single “must” — the divine necessity of the Messiah's mission, from the temple courts in Jerusalem to the ends of the earth.

Jesus's submission to his parents after this episode — “he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them” (v. 51) — is the New Testament's answer to anyone who reads his words in the temple as a claim to be exempt from ordinary human obligations. He is subject to his parents. He grows in wisdom and stature and in favour with God and man (v. 52). The eternal Son of God genuinely grows. This is the mystery of the incarnation: the one who knows all things grows in knowledge; the one who is all-powerful grows in stature; the one in whom all wisdom dwells grows in wisdom. The incarnation is not a costume; it is real human life, lived fully from the inside.
verseByVerse.examples:
Mary and Joseph “did not understand the saying that he spoke to them” (v. 50) — and Mary “treasured up all these things in her heart” (v. 51). For the second time in the chapter, Luke shows us Mary holding what she does not yet understand, refusing to let go of it, waiting for the understanding to come. This is one of the most honest and one of the most encouraging pictures of faith in the entire Gospel: the mother of the Son of God does not always understand what he is doing. But she does not discard what she does not understand. She keeps it, ponders it, waits. The Christian who is honest enough to say “I don't understand this yet” and faithful enough to keep holding it anyway is walking in Mary's tradition.

The closing verse — “And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favour with God and man” — is the New Testament's summary of the hidden years. Eighteen years of silence before the public ministry begins. Eighteen years of growing, learning, working, being formed. The God who could have compressed everything into the three years of public ministry chose instead to spend thirty years in ordinariness. This is the pattern of divine formation: the long preparation, the hidden years, the slow work of wisdom and character before the public work begins. The person who wants to skip the hidden years and get to the public ministry has not yet understood how God shapes those he uses.

verseByVerse.quote: Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the Feast of the Passover. And when he was twelve years old, they went up according to custom. And when the feast was ended, as they were returning, the boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem. His parents did not know it... and when they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem, searching for him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The only story from Jesus's childhood preserved in the Gospels. The family observes the Passover pilgrimage faithfully and annually. Travelling in a large group, Mary and Joseph assume Jesus is somewhere in the caravan. The discovery that he is not there — after a full day's travel — produces three days of anxious searching. Three days: Luke will use that number again. The family's obedient practice of the law is the context in which the first recorded crisis of Jesus's ministry occurs.

verseByVerse.quote: After three days they found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. And all who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers.
verseByVerse.commentary: They find him not lost but engaged — sitting among Jerusalem's teachers, listening and questioning in the standard form of Jewish learning. The teachers are amazed at his understanding. A twelve-year-old is not supposed to be holding his own with the scholars of the capital. Luke says he was listening and asking questions — the posture of a learner — but the learner's understanding exceeds what the teachers expect. The wisdom noted in v. 40 is now publicly visible.

verseByVerse.quote: And when his parents saw him, they were astonished. And his mother said to him, 'Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in great distress.' And he said to them, 'Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?' And they did not understand the saying that he spoke to them.
verseByVerse.commentary: Mary's rebuke is entirely parental: your father and I have been searching for you in great distress. Jesus's response is the first recorded speech of his life — and it is a gentle but clear correction of her categories. Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house? The must (dei) marks divine necessity. Jesus is not being disobedient; he is being exactly where the Father's business requires him to be. But they do not understand. Even Mary, who has treasured and pondered everything, does not yet grasp this. The mystery of who Jesus is exceeds what even the closest observers can contain.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them. And his mother treasured up all these things in her heart. And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favour with God and man.
verseByVerse.commentary: The twelve-year-old who just corrected his mother's categories returns to Nazareth and is obedient to his parents. This is not contradiction — it is the incarnation lived from the inside. The Son of God who must be about his Father's business submits to his earthly parents, because his Father's business includes the full expression of genuine, obedient humanity. He grows in wisdom, stature, and favour with God and man: real growth, real development, real childhood — lived perfectly, preparing everything that is to come.

3.title: The Voice and the Son
3.overview:
Chapter 3 marks the formal beginning of the story Luke has been preparing for since chapter 1. Thirty years have passed in a single verse (2:52). Now the word of God comes to John in the wilderness, and the ministry of preparation begins. Luke anchors the moment in history with a precision unmatched anywhere in the Gospels: the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, the governorship of Pontius Pilate, the tetrarchies of Herod and Philip and Lysanias, the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas. Six named officials, layered like the rings of a tree, establishing exactly when the word of God broke in. Luke the historian is insisting: this happened. You can date it. You can place it. It is not legend.

John's ministry is introduced through Isaiah 40 — “the voice of one crying in the wilderness” — establishing that his role is not to be the destination but the signpost. He is the voice; another is the Word. His message is the message of the prophet: repent, be baptised, bear fruits worthy of repentance. The crowds who come to him receive not comfort but confrontation: “You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?” John is the great deflater of religious presumption — the man who tells Israel that Abrahamic descent is not a sufficient credential before the coming Judge. The axe is at the root of the trees. The one who comes after him will separate the wheat from the chaff with an unquenchable fire.

The chapter ends with two moments of quiet immensity: the baptism of Jesus, where the Trinity is revealed in a form no theologian could have anticipated — the Son in the water, the Spirit as a dove, the Father's voice from heaven — and the genealogy, which traces Jesus's lineage back through David, through Abraham, through Adam, to God himself. Luke's genealogy runs in the opposite direction from Matthew's and reaches further back: not just to Abraham (the Father of Israel) but to Adam (the father of the human race). Jesus is not merely the King of the Jews; he is the son of Adam come to undo what Adam did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — John the Baptist Prepares the Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke opens the public ministry narrative with a synchronism — a dating device borrowed from the great historians of the ancient world, who anchored their narratives in the reigns of known rulers. Six officials are named: Tiberius Caesar (emperor), Pontius Pilate (governor of Judea), Herod Antipas (tetrarch of Galilee), Philip (tetrarch of Iturea and Trachonitis), Lysanias (tetrarch of Abilene), and the high priests Annas and Caiaphas. This is the world into which the word of God intrudes — the world of Roman imperial power, Jewish client kings, and compromised religious leadership. And the word comes not to any of these but to John, in the wilderness, the son of Zechariah. The contrast is pointed: all the power of the world is irrelevant to God's timing. The word comes when God is ready, to whom God chooses, in the place that power ignores.

John's message is structured around three elements. First, a call to baptism for the forgiveness of sins — a ritual immersion that was not invented by John (Jewish proselyte baptism was already practised) but which John radically reapplied: he baptised Jews. In the Jewish world, baptism was for Gentile converts coming into the covenant people. John's baptism of Jews implied that being Jewish was not sufficient — that Israel itself needed to undergo the conversion of repentance. This was scandalous. Second, a confrontation with the crowd's presumption: “Do not begin to say to yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father.' For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.” Ethnic heritage is not a substitute for personal repentance. Third, practical instruction to specific groups: the crowd (share your tunic and food), tax collectors (collect no more than authorised), soldiers (do not extort money, do not accuse falsely, be content with your wages). John's repentance is not abstract; it has hands and feet and specific social implications.

The climax of John's ministry in Luke is not his own proclamation but his announcement of the Coming One: “He who is mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptise you with the Holy Spirit and fire.” John draws a sharp contrast between his own water baptism (the sign of repentance) and the Coming One's baptism of Spirit and fire (the reality of purification and judgment). The one who follows John is not an upgraded version of John; he is categorically greater — a different order of being altogether. John is the last and greatest of the prophets; the one who comes after him is the fulfilment toward which all the prophets pointed. John's ministry ends — in Luke's narrative — before Jesus's baptism is described: Herod arrests him for confronting him over his marriage to his brother's wife. The voice is silenced before the Word begins to speak publicly. The herald makes way for the King.
verseByVerse.theology:
John's declaration that God can raise up children to Abraham from stones is the most radical possible challenge to the theology of ethnic privilege. It disconnects the promise from the bloodline and reconnects it to faith and repentance. This is not the abolition of the covenant with Abraham; it is the clarification of what that covenant always meant. Paul will develop the same argument in Galatians 3 and Romans 4: the true children of Abraham are those who share Abraham's faith, not merely Abraham's biology. John stands at the hinge of the covenants and announces what the new covenant will make explicit: the community of God is defined by repentance and faith, not by descent.

The baptism of the Holy Spirit and fire announces two aspects of the Coming One's work that belong together. The Holy Spirit is the agent of new birth, renewal, and the fulfilment of Joel's promise (Acts 2:17–21). Fire is the agent of purification — the refiner's fire that burns away the dross and the thresher's fire that consumes the chaff. For those who receive him, the Spirit is the fire that purifies; for those who reject him, it is the fire of judgment. John does not separate these two aspects; they are the two sides of the one coming of the King. Every person who encounters Jesus will be touched by fire — the only question is whether it is the fire of purification or the fire of judgment.
verseByVerse.examples:
John's practical instruction to the crowds, the tax collectors, and the soldiers is one of the clearest demonstrations in the Gospels that repentance is not a feeling but a change of behaviour. The crowd asks “what shall we do?” and the answer is not “attend synagogue more faithfully” or “pray more earnestly” — it is “share your tunic and your food.” The tax collector's repentance looks like honest accounting. The soldier's repentance looks like honest soldiering. Genuine repentance always takes the shape of the specific sin it is turning from. The person who claims to have repented but whose behaviour is unchanged has not yet understood what repentance is.

John's willingness to confront Herod Antipas over his adulterous marriage to Herodias (v. 19) — knowing that it would cost him his freedom and eventually his life — is the model of prophetic courage in the face of political power. He does not reserve his confrontational message for the crowds who can do him no harm; he takes it all the way to the palace. The man who tells the crowd hard truths but says comfortable things to the powerful has not yet learned from John. The gospel is not less true in the presence of those who can punish you for speaking it.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea... the word of God came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary: Six named rulers in order of precedence — Caesar, governor, tetrarchs, high priests — and then the word of God bypasses all of them and comes to John in the wilderness. The structure makes a theological argument: the power of the world sits in its palaces, and God addresses none of them. He speaks into the margins, to a man in the desert. The wilderness, not the palace, is where the word of God arrives. It was always so: Moses, Elijah, the prophets — the word of God has always come to the unlikely person in the unlikely place.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went into all the region around the Jordan, proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet, 'The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight...'
verseByVerse.commentary: John's message has one content and one geography: repentance, by the Jordan. The Jordan crossing is Israel's entry into the land; John stands at the river calling people to a new beginning. The quotation of Isaiah 40:3 identifies John as the voice of the Isaianic forerunner. This is not a new religious movement; it is the fulfilment of what the prophets announced. The wilderness, the Jordan, the repentance call — these are deliberate echoes of Israel's foundational story, now arriving at their appointed fulfilment.

verseByVerse.quote: Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be made low, and the crooked shall become straight, and the rough places shall become level ways, and all flesh shall see the salvation of God.
verseByVerse.commentary: Luke includes the verses of Isaiah 40 that Matthew and Mark omit, and the crucial addition is the final line: all flesh shall see the salvation of God. The universality that runs through Luke's Gospel sounds here at its very opening. The road being prepared is not for Israel alone; it is for all peoples. John's ministry at the Jordan is the beginning of a salvation that has no ethnic or geographic boundary. This is why Luke traces the genealogy of Jesus back to Adam rather than Abraham: the scope is universal from the start.

verseByVerse.quote: He said therefore to the crowds that came out to be baptised by him, 'You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Bear fruits in keeping with repentance. And do not begin to say to yourselves, "We have Abraham as our father." For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The crowds come for baptism and receive a challenge to their presumed security. The warning against Abraham-presumption is one of the most radical things in John's preaching: descent from Abraham confers no automatic standing before God. Lineage is not the same as faith. Ritual is not the same as repentance. The axe is at the root — not trimming branches but threatening the whole tree. This is not a gentle prelude to the gospel; it is the exposure of the human condition that makes the gospel necessary.

verseByVerse.quote: And the crowds asked him, 'What then shall we do?' And he answered them, 'Whoever has two tunics is to share with him who has none, and whoever has food is to do likewise.' Tax collectors also came... And soldiers also asked him... And he said to them, 'Do not extort money from anyone by threats or by false accusation, and be content with your wages.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Three groups ask the same question — what shall we do? — and receive direct, practical answers about money and justice. Share your tunic. Collect only what is authorised. Do not extort. John's fruit of repentance is not a new religious programme but a fundamentally reordered relationship with money and neighbours. The tax collectors and soldiers receive specific instructions that cut to the exact temptations of their professions. Repentance that does not change the wallet has not reached the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: As the people were in expectation, and all were questioning in their hearts concerning John, whether he might be the Christ, John answered them all, saying, 'I baptise you with water, but he who is mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptise you with the Holy Spirit and fire.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Popular expectation has reached the point of wondering whether John himself might be the Messiah. His response is immediate: he points entirely away from himself. His baptism is water; the coming one's baptism is Spirit and fire. The contrast is between a preparatory sign and its transforming reality. John has nothing to offer except announcement. The Spirit poured out and the dross burned away — what follows the announcement will be qualitatively different from everything that preceded it.

verseByVerse.quote: But Herod the tetrarch, who had been reproved by him for Herodias, his brother's wife, and for all the evil things that Herod had done, added this to them all, and shut up John in prison.
verseByVerse.commentary: Luke places John's imprisonment before the baptism of Jesus to close the account of John's ministry before Jesus's ministry begins. The pattern is significant: the forerunner ends in prison; the one he announced has everything still before him. Herod's silencing of John is not a footnote — it is a portent. The powers of this age do not welcome the word of God. They silence it when they can. But shutting up the voice does not stop what the voice announced from arriving.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The baptism of Jesus is narrated with remarkable brevity in Luke — briefer even than in Mark. Luke does not linger on the event itself; he focuses on what happens while Jesus is praying after the baptism. This is characteristic of Luke's Gospel: he consistently shows Jesus at prayer at the great turning points of his ministry (3:21; 6:12; 9:18; 9:28; 11:1; 22:41). The baptism is not the centre; the prayer is. And what happens in the prayer is the most explicit Trinitarian moment in the Synoptic Gospels: the Son in the water, praying; the Holy Spirit descending on him in bodily form like a dove; and the Father's voice from heaven: “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.”

Why is Jesus baptised? John's baptism was a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins — and Jesus has no sins to repent of. Matthew records John's protest and Jesus's response: “Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness” (Matthew 3:15). Jesus is baptised not because he needs what baptism signifies but because he is identifying himself with the sinful people he has come to save. He enters the water of repentance as the representative of those who need to repent; he will enter the waters of death as the representative of those who deserve to die. The baptism at the Jordan is the first act of the substitution that will reach its climax at Golgotha.

The Father's voice speaks words that are a weaving together of two Old Testament texts: Psalm 2:7 (“You are my Son; today I have begotten you”) and Isaiah 42:1 (“Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights”). The first is the royal psalm of the Davidic king; the second is the first of the Servant Songs. Jesus is simultaneously the royal Son of David and the suffering Servant of Isaiah — the King who will rule and the Servant who will suffer. Both identities are given to him at his baptism, and the whole of his ministry will be the working out of what it means to be both at once.
verseByVerse.theology:
The descent of the Holy Spirit “in bodily form, like a dove” is Luke's careful insistence that this was a visible, physical event — not a vision or an internal experience but something that could have been witnessed by anyone present. The dove has a complex symbolic background: the dove of Noah that signals the end of judgment (Genesis 8:8–12), the dove of Israel's purity offerings (Leviticus 1:14; 5:7), the dove of the Song of Songs (1:15; 2:14). Most significantly, the Spirit hovering over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2) uses a word that in later Jewish interpretation was associated with the image of a bird brooding over its nest. The Spirit's descent on Jesus signals a new creation — the beginning of the world made new.

The Father's declaration “with you I am well pleased” (en soi eudokēsa) is the announcement of the Father's delight before Jesus has performed a single public miracle, before he has preached a single sermon, before the crowds have approved of him. The Father's pleasure in the Son is not contingent on performance; it is the expression of the eternal love that existed between Father and Son before the foundation of the world (John 17:24). This is the theological foundation of grace: the beloved Son is beloved before he does anything to earn it. And the Christian who is in Christ shares this status — not earned but given, not contingent but settled.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus's baptism while praying is Luke's first instance of a pattern that runs throughout his Gospel: the great moments of Jesus's ministry are set in the context of prayer. The implication is not that prayer causes the Spirit to descend, as if prayer were the mechanism; it is that prayer is the posture of the one who depends entirely on the Father rather than on his own resources. The Son of God prays before every major act of his ministry — not because he lacks information or power but because prayer is the expression of the relationship that defines him. The disciple who prays before major decisions and transitions is not merely following a technique; he is following his Lord.

The Trinity — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — is present at the baptism in a way that is impossible to mistake, yet impossible to fully systematise. The three are distinct: the Son is in the water; the Spirit descends; the Father speaks from heaven. The three are simultaneously present, simultaneously active, simultaneously oriented toward the one redemptive event. The doctrine of the Trinity is not a philosophical puzzle invented by later councils; it is the description of what actually happened at the Jordan. The church simply tried to find words adequate to what Luke and Matthew and Mark describe.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when all the people were baptised, and when Jesus also had been baptised and was praying, the heavens were opened, and the Holy Spirit descended on him in bodily form, like a dove; and a voice came from heaven, 'You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Luke's account differs from the other Gospels in one characteristic detail: Jesus is praying when the heavens open. The Spirit descends in bodily form — Luke insists on the physicality of it. The voice from heaven draws on two texts: You are my beloved Son (Ps. 2:7) and with you I am well pleased (Isa. 42:1). Jesus is at once the Messianic King of Psalm 2 and the Suffering Servant of Isaiah 42. Both identities will be fully lived out in everything that follows. The Father speaks; the Son is affirmed; the Spirit rests. The Trinity is present at the inauguration of the Son's public mission.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–38 — The Genealogy of Jesus Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke's genealogy is unlike Matthew's in three decisive ways: it runs backward (from Jesus to Adam rather than from Abraham to Jesus), it is positioned after the baptism rather than before the birth narrative, and it extends to Adam rather than stopping at Abraham. These differences are not errors or inconsistencies; they are theological choices of the first order. Matthew writes for a Jewish audience and presents Jesus as the fulfilment of Israel's covenant story, beginning with Abraham, ending with the Messiah. Luke writes for a Gentile audience and presents Jesus as the fulfilment of the human story, beginning at the Jordan (where Jesus's identity has just been declared by the Father) and tracing his lineage all the way back to Adam — and beyond Adam, to God himself.

The genealogy also differs from Matthew's in a number of the names listed, particularly in the line between David and Joseph. Many scholars attribute this to Luke tracing the line through Mary rather than Joseph (Godet, Geldenhuys), or to Luke following the legal line of succession while Matthew follows the biological (or vice versa), or to the complexities of levirate marriage in the ancient world. No solution is without difficulty, and the church has lived with the two genealogies for two thousand years without resolving every detail. What is clear is that Luke intends both the royal Davidic descent and the universal human solidarity: Jesus is heir to David's throne and heir to Adam's humanity.

The placement of the genealogy after the baptism, where the Father has just declared “You are my Son,” gives the list its theological frame. The genealogy answers the implicit question: whose son, exactly? He is the son of Joseph (as registered, v. 23) — but Joseph is not really his father. He is the son of David, establishing his royal credentials. He is the son of Abraham, establishing his covenantal credentials. He is the son of Adam, establishing his human solidarity. And he is — the genealogy ends — the son of God. The same title the Father used at the baptism appears at the end of the list as the ultimate origin and identity of the one who stands in the Jordan. He is the son of God who has become the son of Adam so that the sons of Adam might become the sons of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The genealogy ending in “son of Adam, son of God” is Luke's most compact statement of the theology of the incarnation. Jesus traces his human lineage to the first human, establishing the full solidarity of his humanity with every person who has ever lived. He did not merely appear in human form; he entered the long human story at its most specific and particular point — with a real genealogy, real ancestors, real history. This is what Paul means in Galatians 4:4: “born of woman, born under the law” — fully embedded in the human situation he has come to redeem.

The contrast between Adam and Jesus implicit in the genealogy will become explicit in Romans 5:12–21 and 1 Corinthians 15:21–22, 45–49. Adam brought death; the second Adam brings life. Adam's disobedience constituted many sinners; the second Adam's obedience will constitute many righteous. Luke's genealogy does not spell out this typology — that is Paul's work — but it establishes the premise: Jesus is the son of Adam, which means that Adam's story is part of Jesus's story, and Jesus's story is the answer to Adam's story.
verseByVerse.examples:
The genealogy has traditionally been one of those portions of Scripture that readers skip in personal Bible reading — the long list of unfamiliar names seeming like a necessary but uninspiring prelude to the interesting material. But the genealogy is the gospel in miniature: it announces that the salvation of the world comes not through power or privilege but through the long, winding, sometimes scandalous history of real human families and real human choices. Every name in the list is a person whose choices and circumstances contributed to the moment when the Son of God stood in the Jordan. God works through history, through family, through the ordinary and extraordinary decisions of ordinary and extraordinary people. The genealogy is the evidence that providence is not abstract; it is as specific as a name.

The final phrase — “the son of Adam, the son of God” — is the theological summary of everything Luke's Gospel will demonstrate. Jesus is fully human (son of Adam) and fully divine (son of God), and the two identities cannot be separated without destroying the gospel. A Jesus who is only divine cannot save us because he cannot represent us; a Jesus who is only human cannot save us because he has no righteousness to give. The Jesus of Luke's genealogy — rooted in human history all the way back to Eden and identified by the Father as his Son — is the only Jesus who can do what needs to be done.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, when he began his ministry, was about thirty years of age, being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph, the son of Heli... the son of Adam, the son of God.
verseByVerse.commentary: Luke's genealogy runs backwards from Jesus to Adam — the reverse of Matthew's forward genealogy from Abraham. The difference is theological. Matthew establishes Jesus's credentials within Jewish history; Luke establishes his significance for all humanity. The genealogy ends not with Abraham but with Adam, the son of God — connecting Jesus to the beginning of the human race. He is not merely the fulfilment of Israel's hopes; he is the second Adam, the one who will undo what the first Adam did (cf. Rom. 5:12–21). The parenthetical as was supposed regarding Joseph preserves the virgin birth while establishing Jesus's legal lineage within the Davidic line.

4.title: The Testing and the Anointing
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is the chapter of beginnings and confrontations. It opens with the Spirit leading Jesus into the wilderness for forty days of testing — the place where Israel repeatedly failed, now entered by Israel's true representative who will not fail. It continues with the dramatic scene in the Nazareth synagogue where Jesus reads from Isaiah 61 and announces that the Scripture has been fulfilled in their hearing — only to be driven out of the town by the same people who had initially marvelled at him. And it concludes with a succession of healings and exorcisms in Capernaum that demonstrate in action what the Isaiah text announced in words: the kingdom of God has come.

The temptation narrative (vv. 1–13) is the interpretive key to the whole of Jesus's ministry. The devil offers Jesus three things — bread, power, and supernatural protection — and each offer is a shortcut around the path of obedience and suffering that leads to the cross. Jesus refuses each offer with the word of Scripture, demonstrating that the weapons of his warfare are not the weapons of power but the word of God and trust in the Father. The one who overcomes the devil in the wilderness will face him again, in various guises, throughout the ministry — and will face him definitively in the garden of Gethsemane and on the cross. The wilderness is not the final battle; it is the first.

The Nazareth sermon (vv. 14–30) is Luke's programmatic statement of Jesus's mission — the equivalent of the Sermon on the Mount in Matthew. Luke places it at the beginning of the public ministry as the manifesto of the kingdom: good news to the poor, liberty to the captives, sight to the blind, freedom for the oppressed, the year of the Lord's favour. The question the sermon raises — who is included in the “year of the Lord's favour”? — is answered by two Old Testament examples that the congregation finds intolerable: Elijah went not to an Israelite widow but to a Sidonian one; Elisha healed not an Israelite leper but a Syrian one. The good news of the kingdom is for the excluded, the foreigner, the unexpected. This is the gospel Luke has been writing toward since chapter 1 — and the congregation's response is homicidal rage.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The temptation of Jesus follows immediately on the baptism — the Spirit who descended on him at the Jordan now leads him into the wilderness for forty days. The sequence is deliberate and important: the Father's declaration of sonship (“You are my beloved Son”) is immediately followed by the devil's challenge to that sonship (“If you are the Son of God...”). The wilderness is the place where the identity given at the baptism is tested, where the question of what kind of Son Jesus will be is answered. Will he use his divine power for his own benefit? Will he seek the world's kingdoms by the world's methods? Will he test the Father's protection to prove the Father's love? The answer to all three is the same: No. And the “no” is spoken not with supernatural power but with the word of Scripture.

The three temptations correspond to the three great failures of Israel in the wilderness. Israel hungered and grumbled against God (Exodus 16); Jesus is tempted to turn stones to bread. Israel tested God at Massah (Exodus 17:1–7); Jesus is tempted to throw himself from the temple pinnacle. Israel worshipped the golden calf (Exodus 32); Jesus is tempted to bow to Satan in exchange for the kingdoms of the world. At every point where Israel failed, Jesus succeeds — not by an act of raw divine power but by the same means available to every Israelite: the word of God, received, believed, and obeyed. He quotes three times from Deuteronomy — the book Moses gave to Israel before they entered the promised land, the book of covenant faithfulness in the face of temptation.

The devil's final offer — supernatural protection based on a proof-text from Psalm 91 — is the most subtle of the three. The devil has learned to quote Scripture, and he quotes it accurately. The temptation is not to misread the promise but to use the promise as leverage — to demand that the Father demonstrate his care by preventing the consequences of a foolish act. Jesus's response — “You shall not put the Lord your God to the test” — draws on Deuteronomy 6:16, the passage about Israel's testing at Massah. The difference between trust and testing is the difference between resting in God's faithfulness and demanding that God prove it on our terms. The person who says “I'll believe God loves me if he does this specific thing” is not trusting God; they are testing him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The temptation narrative establishes Jesus as the second Adam as well as the true Israel. Adam was tempted in a garden of abundance and failed; Jesus is tempted in a wilderness of deprivation and succeeds. Adam's failure introduced sin and death into the human story; Jesus's victory begins the reversal. This is the theological logic Paul unpacks in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15: what the first Adam lost, the second Adam wins back. But the victory is not won by supernatural force; it is won by the very means God made available to Adam — the word of God and the decision to trust it rather than the serpent's alternative.

The devil's departure “until an opportune time” (v. 13) is Luke's signal that the temptation narrative is not over — it continues through the ministry in the form of opposition from demons, from religious leaders, from the crowd's desire to make Jesus a political king. The final “opportune time” is the passion: “Then Satan entered into Judas” (22:3); “This is your hour, and the power of darkness” (22:53). The wilderness is the opening skirmish; the cross is the decisive battle. But at the cross, what looks like Satan's victory is the moment of his defeat — the Son who refused every shortcut in the wilderness walks through the full cost of obedience to its end.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus's weapon against every temptation is the word of Scripture — received, remembered, and spoken with precision. He does not argue philosophically; he does not marshal emotional responses; he does not call on supernatural resources unavailable to ordinary disciples. He quotes the word of God. This is not a pastoral cliché; it is a pattern with enormous practical implications. The Christian who has stored up the word of God — who knows it, who has prayed it, who has thought about it — has access to the same weapon Jesus used. The Christian who has neglected the word is left to fight with whatever arguments they can produce on the spot, which is fighting with water pistols against a military opponent.

The devil quotes Psalm 91 — accurately. The church has always known that the most dangerous misuse of Scripture is not the obviously wrong use but the superficially plausible use — taking a true promise out of its covenantal context and using it to justify something the covenant forbids. Every cult, every aberrant theology, every moral failure that has been sanctioned by a proof-text illustrates this danger. The Christian who knows not just individual verses but the shape of the whole biblical narrative is equipped to recognise when Scripture is being used against its own purposes.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness for forty days, being tempted by the devil.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Spirit who descended at the baptism now leads Jesus into the wilderness — not away from God but deeper into the Father's purpose. The Spirit does not protect Jesus from testing; He conducts him into it. The forty days echo Israel's forty years in the wilderness, where the nation failed repeatedly. Jesus goes where Israel went and will do what Israel could not do. He is not tested despite the Spirit's leading; he is tested because of it. The obedience that qualifies him to be Saviour must be demonstrated under the hardest conditions.

verseByVerse.quote: The devil said to him, 'If you are the Son of God, command this stone to become bread.' And Jesus answered him, 'It is written, "Man shall not live by bread alone."'
verseByVerse.commentary: The first temptation strikes at physical need after forty days of fasting. If you are the Son of God — a challenge to prove identity through the use of power for personal benefit. Jesus refuses not because bread is wrong but because this bread, obtained this way, at this moment, would be a defection from dependence on the Father. His answer from Deuteronomy 8:3 is Israel's lesson from the wilderness — the lesson Israel never fully learned. Life is not sustained by bread but by the word that comes from the Father's mouth. Jesus lives by that word now, in the wilderness, hungry.

verseByVerse.quote: And the devil took him up and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time, and said to him, 'To you I will give all their authority and their glory... If you, then, will worship me, it will all be yours.' And Jesus answered him, 'It is written, "You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve."'
verseByVerse.commentary: The second temptation offers what the Father has already promised through the cross — dominion over all the kingdoms — but through a shortcut that bypasses the cross entirely. The temptation is to receive the right thing by the wrong means. The devil's claim to authority over the kingdoms is not entirely false (cf. 1 John 5:19), but Jesus will receive all authority through suffering, not around it. He refuses with Deuteronomy 6:13: there is only one worthy of worship, and the devil is not that one.

verseByVerse.quote: And he took him to Jerusalem and set him on the pinnacle of the temple and said to him, 'If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here, for it is written, "He will command his angels concerning you..."' And Jesus answered him, 'It is said, "You shall not put the Lord your God to the test."'
verseByVerse.commentary: The third temptation is the most subtle: the devil quotes Scripture. Psalm 91:11–12 is real, and the promise of angelic protection is real. But the temptation is to force God's hand — to create a situation that requires the promise's fulfilment. This is not faith; it is manipulation wearing the costume of faith. Faith trusts the promise without engineering the circumstances that will require it. Jesus answers with Deuteronomy 6:16, addressing Israel's demand at Massah for proof of God's presence. He will not put the Father to the test.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the devil had ended every temptation, he departed from him until an opportune time.
verseByVerse.commentary: The devil exhausts his arsenal — every temptation — and leaves. But not permanently: until an opportune time. The temptation of Jesus does not end in the wilderness. It resurfaces in Gethsemane (22:28, 40, 46) and at the cross itself (23:35–37). The victory in the wilderness is real but the conflict is ongoing. Jesus will meet the devil's pressure again at every crucial moment of the passion. He will meet it each time the same way: as a son who trusts his Father and does what his Father says.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus returns from the wilderness “in the power of the Spirit” — the forty days of testing have not depleted him; they have confirmed and concentrated his anointing. He teaches in the synagogues throughout Galilee, and everyone praises him. Then he comes to Nazareth, the town where he grew up, and on the Sabbath he stands to read in the synagogue. He is handed the scroll of Isaiah, and he finds the place — Isaiah 61:1–2. “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor.” He reads it, rolls up the scroll, hands it back, and sits down. The eyes of everyone in the synagogue are fixed on him. And he says: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”

The congregation's first response is astonishment: they marvel at the “gracious words” coming from his mouth, and they say “Is not this Joseph's son?” — a reaction that is simultaneously admiring and dismissive. They are impressed by the teacher from their own town; they are not prepared to receive the claim he is making. Jesus reads their response and pre-empts the objection he knows is forming: “Doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, 'Physician, heal yourself.' What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here in your hometown also.” He knows that the familiarity of home is the enemy of reception. A prophet is not accepted in his hometown.

Then he does the thing that turns admiration into murderous fury. He tells them two stories from the Old Testament: Elijah and the widow of Zarephath (1 Kings 17), and Elisha and Naaman the Syrian (2 Kings 5). In both stories, the prophet bypassed Israelites in need and brought God's blessing to a Gentile. Elijah could have gone to any of the widows in Israel; he went to a pagan widow in Sidon. Elisha could have cleansed any of the lepers in Israel; he cleansed a Syrian general. The point is clear, and the congregation hears it perfectly: the year of the Lord's favour is not automatically theirs. They could be the Israelites who were passed over while the blessing went to the outsider. This is a challenge to every form of religious privilege — and the response of those who feel their privilege threatened is exactly what you would expect: they rise up, drive Jesus out of town, and attempt to throw him off a cliff. Jesus walks through the midst of them and goes away.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Isaiah 61 text Jesus reads is a Jubilee text — the year of the Lord's favour is the Year of Jubilee, the fiftieth year when debts were cancelled, slaves were freed, and land returned to its original owners (Leviticus 25). Jesus announces that the ultimate Jubilee has arrived — not an economic reset but a cosmic one: the debt of sin cancelled, the captivity to Satan ended, the blind given sight, the oppressed set free. The Jubilee that Israel's economic system pointed toward is now happening in the person of the one who reads about it. This is why he can say “today” — not “soon” or “when the conditions are right” but today, in your hearing.

The rage of the Nazareth congregation at the Elijah and Elisha stories is the rage of religious privilege challenged. They wanted a Messiah for Israel who would bless Israel and defeat Israel's enemies — not a Messiah who would take the blessing to the enemies themselves. Every generation of the church faces the same temptation: to want Jesus for itself, to treat the gospel as the property of those who already have it, to be astonished and offended when the grace of God reaches the people we had written off. The Nazareth synagogue is the constant warning against a Christianity that has lost the scandal of grace.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” is the most decisive “today” in all of Luke's Gospel — and Luke's Gospel is full of “todays”: “unto you is born this day a Saviour” (2:11); “today salvation has come to this house” (19:9); “today you will be with me in Paradise” (23:43). The “today” of the gospel is always urgent, always present, always immediate. The Scripture fulfilled in Jesus is not fulfilled in some spiritual realm that has no connection to the present moment; it is fulfilled now, here, in the hearing of specific people in a specific place. The gospel is always a present-tense announcement, never merely a past-tense history or a future-tense hope.

Jesus walking through the crowd that intends to kill him (v. 30) is the first of several moments in Luke where Jesus moves through danger without harm — not because violence is ineffective but because his hour has not yet come. This is the sovereign protection of providential timing: he cannot be killed before the moment appointed for his death, because his death must be the death he chooses, on the terms the Father has set, for the purposes the Father has determined. The attempted murder at Nazareth fails not because Jesus escapes by clever means but because divine necessity governs the timing of his death.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee, and a report about him went out through all the surrounding country. And he taught in their synagogues, being glorified by all.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus went into the wilderness full of the Spirit (v. 1); he returns in the power of the Spirit. The testing has not diminished him. The report spreading through the whole country is Luke's compressed account of a period of ministry that John's Gospel describes in more detail. The initial reception is positive — glorified by all. That welcome is about to be severely tested in the town where he grew up.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. And as was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and he stood up to read. And the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. He unrolled the scroll and found the place where it was written, 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor...'
verseByVerse.commentary: Luke places the Nazareth scene at the opening of the public ministry as its programmatic statement. Jesus is given the Isaiah scroll and reads Isaiah 61:1–2, the great anointing text of the Servant of the LORD. The Spirit who descended at the baptism and led through the wilderness has anointed him for a specific task: good news to the poor, release to captives, sight to the blind, freedom for the oppressed, the year of Jubilee. This is not an abstract agenda; it is a description of what the next chapters of Luke will contain, scene by scene.

verseByVerse.quote: And he rolled up the scroll and gave it back to the attendant and sat down. And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. And he began to say to them, 'Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Today. Not soon, not eventually — today, in your hearing, before these people, in this town. The word today (sēmeron) is one of Luke's characteristic words for the realised presence of salvation (2:11; 19:9; 23:43). The scroll has been read; the reader has declared himself the one the text describes. The silence in the synagogue at this declaration must have been absolute. The eyes of all were fixed on him — and they are about to see what he means by it.

verseByVerse.quote: And all spoke well of him and marvelled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth. And they said, 'Is not this Joseph's son?' And he said to them, 'Doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, "Physician, heal yourself."... And he said, 'Truly, I say to you, no prophet is acceptable in his hometown.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The initial response is favourable — the townspeople are impressed — but the compliment contains the problem: Is not this Joseph's son? Familiarity breeds a kind of contempt harder to penetrate than open hostility. Jesus reads the room and confronts the unspoken demand: they want a local display of miracles. He refuses, and names the refusal as a prophetic pattern. No prophet is accepted in his hometown. He is not surprised; he is simply honest about what is happening.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But in truth, I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah... yet Elijah was sent to none of them but only to Zarephath... to a woman who was a widow. And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus reaches back to the most uncomfortable episodes in the prophetic tradition: Elijah sent to a Gentile widow; Elisha healing a Syrian general while Israelite lepers went uncleansed. Both examples make the same point: the grace of God is not the exclusive property of those who are geographically or culturally nearest to it. God has always moved outside the boundaries his people drew around his activity. The implication for Nazareth is clear, and it is not welcome.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath. And they rose up and drove him out of the town and brought him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built, so that they could throw him down the cliff. But passing through their midst, he went away.
verseByVerse.commentary: The congregation's mood reverses entirely — from admiration to murderous rage — in the space of two verses. The exposure of Israel's assumption of preferential treatment is intolerable. They drive him to the cliff edge. But the hour has not yet come: passing through their midst, he went away. No miracle is described; Jesus simply passes through. The rejection at Nazareth is a miniature of the larger rejection that will come in Jerusalem — and like that rejection, it does not prevent what God has determined to accomplish.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
From Nazareth — where he was rejected — Jesus goes to Capernaum, which will become the base of his Galilean ministry. In Capernaum, within what appears to be a single Sabbath day, he teaches in the synagogue with authority, exorcises an unclean spirit, heals Simon Peter's mother-in-law, and at sunset heals a multitude of sick and demon-possessed people who have been brought to him. The contrast with Nazareth is complete: the hometown that rejected him is replaced by a city that receives him, and the result is a cascade of kingdom power — teaching, healing, and liberation from demonic oppression.

The unclean spirit in the synagogue is Luke's first exorcism, and it raises a question that will run through the whole Gospel: what is the relationship between the kingdom of God and the realm of demons? The demon's recognition of Jesus — “What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are — the Holy One of God” — is the first correct christological confession in Luke's Gospel, and it comes from a demon. The demonic world recognises Jesus before the human world does; the powers of darkness know that his arrival means their destruction. Jesus silences the demon and casts it out with a word — no ritual, no incantation, no elaborate procedure. The word of the King is enough.

The healing of Peter's mother-in-law (vv. 38–39) is narrated with the same economy as the exorcism: Jesus “rebuked” the fever (the same verb used for the exorcism), and it left her. The response is immediate: she rises and serves them. This is the New Testament pattern of healing and restoration — the one who has been restored begins immediately to give. The woman who receives healing becomes the woman who provides hospitality. Restored life immediately seeks expression in service. The healing at sunset — when the Sabbath ended and it was lawful to carry the sick through the streets — is the picture of the kingdom in miniature: the whole city gathered at the door, and Jesus healing them one by one, laying hands on each one.
verseByVerse.theology:
The demon's address — “the Holy One of God” (ho hagios tou theou) — is a title that appears elsewhere in the New Testament only in John 6:69, where Peter confesses it. The irony is devastating: the demon confesses what the disciples will only gradually come to understand, what the religious leaders will refuse to acknowledge. The spiritual world sees what the natural eye misses. But the demon's knowledge does not save it — knowledge of who Jesus is, without submission to who he is, is not faith. The demons believe and tremble (James 2:19); they do not trust and rest.

Jesus's departure from Capernaum “when it was day” to pray in a desolate place (v. 42) — and his response to the crowds who want to keep him from leaving (“I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns also, for I was sent for this purpose”) — establishes the missionary imperative of the ministry. The crowds want to privatise Jesus: “keep him from going from them.” Jesus refuses. He has been sent to more than Capernaum; the gospel is for more than those who happen to be near. The word “must” (dei) appears again — the same divine necessity that drove him to the temple at twelve, that drove him through the wilderness, that will drive him to Jerusalem. He cannot stay; he was sent for something larger.
verseByVerse.examples:
The demon's terror at the presence of Jesus — “Have you come to destroy us?” — is the correct recognition of what the kingdom of God means for the powers of darkness. Wherever the kingdom comes, the dominion of darkness recedes. This is the cosmic dimension of every act of healing, every exorcism, every act of forgiveness in the Gospels: it is not merely a personal benefit to the recipient but a territorial defeat for the enemy. The church that prays for the sick, that casts out fear and guilt and lies in the name of Jesus, that proclaims forgiveness and freedom — is doing what Jesus did in Capernaum. The war is the same; the weapons are the same.

The crowds “sought to keep him from leaving them” (v. 42). The desire to possess Jesus — to keep him localised, to make him the exclusive property of one community, one congregation, one tradition — is one of the permanent temptations of Christian communities. Jesus consistently resists it. He came not to be kept but to be followed; not to serve one community's needs but to bring the kingdom to every town and village. The congregation that asks “how can we keep Jesus to ourselves?” has asked the wrong question. The right question is “how do we follow him to the next town?”

verseByVerse.quote: And he went down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee. And he was teaching them on the Sabbath, and they were astonished at his teaching, for his word possessed authority.
verseByVerse.commentary: Capernaum receives what Nazareth rejected. Those who think they know Jesus best are least able to receive him; those who encounter him fresh are astonished. The key word is authority (exousia): Jesus does not teach like the scribes, who appeal to other authorities. He teaches as one who is himself the source. His word is not commentary on the tradition; it is the word that the tradition was always pointing toward.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the synagogue there was a man who had the spirit of an unclean demon, and he cried out with a loud voice, 'Ha! What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are — the Holy One of God.' But Jesus rebuked him, saying, 'Be silent and come out of him!'
verseByVerse.commentary: The first miracle in Luke's public ministry is an exorcism, and the demon speaks the truth: I know who you are — the Holy One of God. The demons recognise Jesus before the disciples do, before the religious leaders do, before almost anyone. Their recognition is not reverence; it is terror. They know his arrival means their domain is under attack. Jesus silences the demon — he will accept no testimony from unclean spirits, even accurate testimony — and casts it out with one word. The authority over people in his teaching is the same authority over the spiritual realm in his actions.

verseByVerse.quote: And he arose and left the synagogue and entered Simon's house. Now Simon's mother-in-law was ill with a high fever, and they appealed to him on her behalf. And he stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her, and immediately she rose and began to serve them.
verseByVerse.commentary: From the synagogue to a private home — the authority of Jesus operates in both. He rebukes the fever as he rebuked the demon, with the same word of command. The healing is immediate and complete. And the restored person immediately serves: she rises and begins to wait on them. That pattern — grace producing service, the healed becoming the helper — is the shape of discipleship throughout Luke's Gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the sun was setting, all those who had any who were sick with various diseases brought them to him, and he laid his hands on every one of them and healed them. And demons also came out of many, crying, 'You are the Son of God!' But he rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: At sunset — the end of the Sabbath, when carrying the sick was no longer restricted — the whole town gathers at Simon's door. Jesus heals them individually: every one of them. Not a mass cure at a distance, but a personal laying on of hands for each person. The demons repeat their testimony; he silences them again. His identity will not be announced by unclean spirits. The proclamation must come at the right time, through the right witnesses, in the right way.

verseByVerse.quote: And when it was day, he departed and went into a desolate place. And the people sought him and came to him, and would have kept him from leaving them. But he said to them, 'I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose.' And he was preaching in the synagogues of Judea.
verseByVerse.commentary: After the healings, Jesus withdraws to pray. The crowd tries to keep him; he refuses to be kept. I must (dei) — divine necessity again. He was not sent to Capernaum alone but to the other towns as well. The popularity of a crowd is not the same as the calling of God, and Jesus is never confused about the difference. He goes where he was sent, not where he is wanted. That distinction will define his entire ministry.

5.title: Calling, Cleansing, and the New Wine
5.overview:
Chapter 5 gathers five scenes that together define what it means to encounter Jesus: a miraculous catch of fish that produces not pride but prostration; the cleansing of a man whose disease had made him untouchable; the healing of a paralytic whose friends refused to be stopped by a crowd; the call of a tax collector from his booth; and a dispute about fasting that opens into the deepest question of the chapter — whether the new thing Jesus is doing can be contained in the old structures of Judaism. The answer is no. New wine requires new wineskins. What Jesus brings is not a reform of the old system; it is something genuinely, radically new.

The call of the first disciples (vv. 1–11) is Luke's fullest account of how Peter, James, and John came to follow Jesus — fuller than the brief summaries in Matthew and Mark, because Luke wants to show not just the what but the why. They did not follow a charismatic teacher because he seemed promising. They followed because they had encountered something that simultaneously exposed their unworthiness and compelled their trust. Peter's “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord” is the most honest response to the presence of holiness in the New Testament — the instinct that knows it cannot stand in the presence of what it has just encountered, and is answered not with departure but with the word: “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men.”

The chapter closes with a theological dispute about fasting (vv. 33–39) that turns out to be the interpretive key to everything that has come before. The Pharisees and John's disciples fast; Jesus's disciples do not. The question is not merely about religious practice; it is about eschatology. Jesus answers with the image of a wedding: the bridegroom is present. The time of mourning is over; the feast has begun. This is not the time for old wineskins; the new wine of the kingdom — the presence of the Son of God himself — cannot be contained in the structures designed for a world still waiting for him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Jesus Calls the First Disciples
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The call of the first disciples is set on the shore of the Lake of Gennesaret — the Sea of Galilee — where Simon Peter and his partners James and John have fished all night and caught nothing. Jesus borrows Peter's boat as a floating pulpit, teaches the crowd from the water, and then tells Peter to put out into the deep and let down the nets. The instruction is professionally absurd: fishermen who have worked through the prime fishing hours of the night without result do not take instruction on technique from a carpenter. But Peter obeys — “at your word I will let down the nets” — and the result is a catch so large that both boats begin to sink.

The miracle is not primarily about fish. It is about the person who commanded the catch. Peter, who knows these waters better than almost anyone alive, has just witnessed something that no expert's competence can produce. The response is immediate and instinctive: he falls at Jesus's knees and says “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord.” This is the language of Isaiah's vision (Isaiah 6:5 — “Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips”), of Job's encounter with the whirlwind (Job 42:5–6), of John falling as dead at the feet of the risen Christ (Revelation 1:17). It is the response of a creature who has encountered uncreated holiness and knows, in his bones, that he has no standing there. Peter does not argue the point or minimise his sinfulness; he knows immediately and completely that he is in the presence of something he cannot approach.

Jesus's response to Peter's confession of unworthiness is not agreement or dismissal but calling: “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men.” The fear that the presence of holiness produces is not the end of the encounter; it is the beginning of the commission.
