This is the faith that the church has lived on since the ascension: the one who heals and saves is not physically present, but his word has not changed, and the authority behind his word is exactly what the centurion perceived.
verseByVerse.theology:
The centurion's analogy between military authority and the authority of Jesus is more profound than it first appears. He is not merely saying “Jesus is like a commanding officer.” He is recognising that Jesus's authority over illness and death has the same character as authority in a chain of command: it operates through words, at a distance, on the basis of the relationship between the speaker and the one being commanded. The centurion knows that the soldier who refuses his order is refusing the Roman emperor whose authority he represents. He perceives that the illness that Jesus commands is in the same position — and he is right. The authority Jesus exercises over creation is the authority of its Creator, and creation obeys its Creator.

Jesus's amazement — “he marvelled at him” — is one of only two places in the Gospels where Jesus is said to marvel (the other is at the unbelief of Nazareth, Mark 6:6). The God-man who knows all things is genuinely astonished by the centurion's faith — not because it was unexpected by his divine foreknowledge, but because in his full humanity he encounters something that exceeds what he has seen in Israel. This is a window into the genuine humanity of Jesus: he is truly capable of being surprised, truly capable of encountering something that moves him to wonder.
verseByVerse.examples:
The centurion's self-description — “I am not worthy to have you come under my roof” — is the model of the humility that genuine faith produces. He is, by every external measure, one of the most impressive people in the narrative: he has authority, he has resources, he has a reputation for generosity and love of Israel. And yet he is the one who says “I am not worthy.” The elders of the synagogue say he is worthy; he says he is not. The humility is not false modesty; it is the accurate perception of a man who has understood who he is asking for help. The person who knows who Jesus is cannot help but feel the distance between the petitioner and the one petitioned — and it is precisely this awareness that Jesus names as great faith.

The centurion did not come in person, yet he received everything he asked for. The absence of physical presence did not diminish the efficacy of the word of Jesus — the servant was healed at the same moment the word was spoken. This is the encouragement of every Christian who prays for someone they are separated from by distance: the word of Jesus is not constrained by geography. The authority the centurion trusted across the distance of Capernaum's streets is the same authority trusted across continents and oceans in every generation of the church's prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: When he heard about Jesus, he sent to him elders of the Jews, asking him to come and heal his servant. And when they came to Jesus, they pleaded with him earnestly, saying, 'He is worthy to have you do this for him, for he loves our nation, and he built us our synagogue.'... When Jesus heard these things, he marvelled at him, and turning to the crowd that followed him, said, 'I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The structure of the story is carefully arranged: the centurion sends the Jewish elders (v. 3), then sends friends with his self-deprecating message (v. 6), and the healing happens without Jesus ever reaching the house. Three layers of mediation, yet the healing is direct and immediate. Luke may intend this structure to model the way the gospel will move in Acts: through intermediaries, through unlikely channels, to those who were never the expected recipients — but always with the same efficacy, because the word of the one who sends is the word that heals.

The centurion's concern for his servant (doulos — the word can mean slave or servant) reveals something about his character: he has a valued relationship with someone in his service whose life matters to him. This is not the contemptuous master demanding his property be repaired; this is a man of authority who cares about those in his care. The Luke who writes about the last becoming first, about the overlooked being seen, notices that the man who comes to Jesus for help is coming not for himself but for someone under his authority. The faith that moves Jesus to marvel is interceding faith.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–17 — Jesus Raises a Widow's Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The raising of the widow's son at Nain is one of the most tender scenes in Luke's Gospel — and one of the most deliberately crafted. Two crowds meet at the gate of the town: the crowd following Jesus, and the funeral procession coming out of the town. At the centre of the procession is a widow, carrying out her only son. Luke underlines the detail: she is a widow; this is her only son. In the ancient world, a widow with no male relative was socially and economically destitute — she had no source of income, no legal protection, no advocate. The death of her only son is not merely a grief; it is the end of her future. She has nothing and no one.

Jesus sees her. The Greek is precise: “when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her.” The word “Lord” (ho kyrios) appears here for the first time in Luke's narrative as a title for Jesus in his own right — not just an address from a speaker but Luke's own authorial description of who Jesus is. And this Lord, who sees the widow in the crowd, has compassion: the word is esplagchnisthē — he was moved in his gut, the same visceral, involuntary compassion the Benedictus described as God's character (1:78). He does not wait for a request. She has not asked anything. He simply sees her, is moved, and acts.

He touches the bier — making himself ritually unclean by contact with a coffin — and says: “Young man, I say to you, arise.” The dead man sits up and begins to speak. Luke notes the detail with medical exactitude — sits up, begins to speak — and Jesus gives him to his mother, echoing the exact words of 1 Kings 17:23, where Elijah “gave him to his mother” after raising the widow of Zarephath's son. The crowd's response is awe and glorification of God: “A great prophet has arisen among us!” and “God has visited his people!” Both responses are true — and both fall short. He is not merely a great prophet; he is the Lord of life itself. And God has not merely visited; he has arrived, and with him the power of the age to come.
verseByVerse.theology:
The raising of the widow's son is a sign of the kingdom that has both an immediate and an ultimate reference. Immediately, it is the reversal of the most final of all reversals — death — accomplished by the one who will himself die and rise. Ultimately, it points to the general resurrection of the dead at the last day, when the dead in Christ will rise at the voice of the Son of God (John 5:25–29; 1 Thessalonians 4:16). Jesus does not raise the widow's son permanently — the young man will die again. What the miracle demonstrates is not the conquest of biological death permanently but the authority of the Son of God over death as a power, the authority that will achieve its final expression in the resurrection of Jesus himself.

The echo of Elijah at Zarephath (1 Kings 17:17–24) is deliberate — Luke has already drawn the Elijah-Nazareth connection in 4:26, and now the parallel deepens. Both prophets are confronted with a widow whose only son has died; both speak a word of resurrection; both give the son back to his mother. The echo establishes Jesus as the fulfilment of the prophetic tradition rather than merely its continuation. Where Elijah prayed three times and stretched himself on the boy, Jesus simply speaks. The authority has been concentrated. The prophet gives way to the Lord of the prophets.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus's compassion for the widow, unprompted and unsolicited, is the model of the grace that sees before it is asked. She did not pray; she did not seek Jesus out; she was lost in her grief. He saw her. The God who sees — the El Roi that Hagar named in the wilderness (Genesis 16:13) — is the God who acts on what he sees without waiting for a formal petition. The Christian who prays “open my eyes to see what you see” is praying to become like the Lord who walked through Nain and noticed a widow at the gate of a funeral procession and was moved to act. The posture of compassion begins with seeing.

“Weep not” — the two words Jesus speaks to the widow before he raises her son — are among the most comforting in the Gospel, and among the most demanding. They are not a denial of the grief; they are the anticipation of what is about to happen. He does not say “you should not be weeping” — she has every reason to weep. He says “stop weeping” because the situation is about to change. This is the eschatological comfort of the gospel in every generation: “weep not” is not an instruction to suppress sorrow but the announcement of a coming joy that will transform the sorrow. The comfort of the gospel always points forward to the moment when every tear will be wiped away.

verseByVerse.quote: Soon afterward he went to a town called Nain, and his disciples and a great crowd went with him. As he drew near to the gate of the town, behold, a man who had died was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow... And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her, 'Do not weep.' Then he came up and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still. And he said, 'Young man, I say to you, arise.' And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him to his mother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nain is a small village in the Jezreel Valley, about six miles southeast of Nazareth. It is not mentioned anywhere else in the Old Testament or in Jewish literature of the period — an unimportant place, forgotten between the visits of armies and historians. That Luke records this miracle at Nain is itself a Lukan touch: the most significant event in Nain's history is a resurrection, and it happens because a widow's grief caught the eye of the one passing through. The geography of grace is always being written in places the history books ignore.

The word “arise” (egerthēti) is the resurrection word — the same word used for Jesus's own resurrection in 9:22, 18:33, 24:6, 24:34. Luke's vocabulary choice is not accidental. When Jesus raises the widow's son, he uses the word that will describe his own rising. The authority he exercises over death is the same authority that will be exercised over his own death. The raising at Nain is the small demonstration of the great event toward which the whole Gospel is moving.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–35 — Messengers from John the Baptist
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
John is in prison — Herod has arrested him for confronting the tetrarch's illegal marriage, and the imprisonment has raised the question that was always implicit in John's ministry: if Jesus is the Coming One, why is this happening? John has heard about Jesus's works and sends two of his disciples to ask the question directly: “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?” The question is both the most honest and the most remarkable question in the Gospels. John who announced Jesus from the womb, who saw the Spirit descend at the Jordan, who declared “Behold the Lamb of God” (John 1:29) — this John is in a cell, in the dark, wondering if he was right.

Jesus's answer is not a rebuke or a reassurance but a demonstration: “Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them.” The list is a mosaic of Isaiah's promises about the age of salvation: Isaiah 26:19 (the dead raised), Isaiah 29:18 (deaf hear, blind see), Isaiah 35:5–6 (blind see, deaf hear, lame leap), Isaiah 61:1 (good news to the poor). Jesus is answering John's doubt not with an argument but with evidence — and the evidence is the texts that John knew by heart, now being enacted in history. “And blessed is the one who is not offended by me” — the beatitude is a gentle warning: there is a form of expectation about the Messiah that, when the real Messiah arrives, becomes a stumbling block. John expected the one who would separate the wheat from the chaff with unquenchable fire. What he is getting is healing and good news to the poor. Both are true of Jesus. But the fire will come later.

After the messengers leave, Jesus turns to the crowd and speaks about John — and what he says is an extraordinary tribute. What did you go out to see? A reed shaken by the wind? A man in soft clothing? No — a prophet. And more than a prophet: the messenger of Malachi 3:1, the one who prepares the way. “Among those born of women none is greater than John.” And then the statement that has puzzled readers for two thousand years: “Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.” The greatness of John is the greatness of the greatest Old Testament prophet; the greatness of the least in the kingdom is the greatness of those who live on the other side of the cross and resurrection, who have received what all the prophets longed to see. Position in the kingdom of grace exceeds position in the history of promise, even at its greatest.
verseByVerse.theology:
John's doubt from prison is the New Testament's most honest portrait of faith under pressure — and it is treated with complete respect by Jesus. He does not rebuke John or question his faith; he answers his question with the most careful possible evidence. This is the pastoral heart of the passage: genuine doubt, honestly expressed, receives a genuine answer. The Christian tradition that has sometimes treated doubt as a mark of spiritual failure has missed the pastoral model of Jesus, who addresses John's doubt with evidence rather than with condemnation. Honest wrestling with the question “is it really true?” is not the absence of faith; it is faith that has been pushed to its limit by circumstance and is still asking.

The saying about the least in the kingdom being greater than John is not a demotion of John but an elevation of the kingdom. John stands at the threshold; those who are in the kingdom stand inside it. The least of those who have the Spirit, who know the forgiveness of sins through the cross, who have the hope of the resurrection — they possess something that John, for all his greatness, did not yet have at the moment of his question. The kingdom of God is the sphere in which the full salvation of God is received; to be in it, at any level, is to have something the greatest pre-kingdom prophet did not yet fully possess.
verseByVerse.examples:
John's question from prison is the question of every sincere believer who has faced a crisis of expectation: “I believed this was true; this is not what I expected; am I wrong?” The answer Jesus gives is not “of course you're right, don't worry” — it is “look at the evidence.” The evidence is the Scriptures being fulfilled in front of their eyes. When faith is under pressure, the antidote is not mere reassurance but the careful examination of the evidence — the evidence of Scripture, of history, of the testimony of those who have encountered the risen Christ. Faith is not a leap in the dark; it is a step toward the light of evidence that has been carefully examined.

Jesus's tribute to John as the greatest born of women — and yet the least in the kingdom is greater — is the most encouraging statement for ordinary Christians in the chapter. John was heroic by any measure: courageous, ascetic, single-minded, prophetically gifted. You are the least of those in the kingdom. And yet the grace you have received — the forgiveness of the cross, the indwelling of the Spirit, the hope of the resurrection — exceeds John's possession of those things in his moment of greatest doubt. Do not measure yourself by John's heroism; measure yourself by the kingdom you have been given.

verseByVerse.quote: And John, calling two of his disciples to him, sent them to the Lord, saying, 'Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?' And when the men had come to him, they said, 'John the Baptist has sent us to you, saying, “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?”' In that hour he healed many people of diseases and plagues and evil spirits, and on many who were blind he bestowed sight. And he answered them, 'Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them. And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The one who is to come” (ho erchomenos) was a recognized messianic title in first-century Judaism, based on the language of Psalm 118:26 (“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD”), Malachi 3:1, and other texts. John uses his own vocabulary — he called the Coming One “mightier than I” (3:16) — but the question is clear: is Jesus the one that all the prophets and John himself have been pointing toward? The formulation “or shall we look for another” suggests that the doubt is genuine rather than rhetorical: John is giving himself permission to abandon his testimony if the evidence requires it. This is not epistemic cowardice; it is epistemic honesty.

Jesus heals “in that hour” — in the presence of John's messengers — before he gives his verbal response. He lets them see and hear first; then he tells them to report what they have seen and heard. The verbal testimony is validated by the visible evidence. This is the pattern of apostolic witness in Acts: the proclamation of the word is accompanied by signs that confirm it. The evidence Jesus offers John is not a claim but a demonstration, not an argument but a recital of events that the prophets predicted and that are now happening in front of the messengers' eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: When John's messengers had gone, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John: 'What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who are dressed in splendid clothing and live in luxury are in kings' courts. What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet... I tell you, among those born of women none is greater than John. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rhetorical questions — “what did you go out to see?” — are addressed to the crowd who had followed John into the wilderness. They know what they went to see: not a political weather-vane (a reed shaken by the wind shifts with every breeze, as compliant leaders shift with political pressure), not a courtier in soft clothing (John wore camel's hair — Mark 1:6), but a prophet. Jesus affirms what they knew but extends it: John is more than a prophet because he is the one Malachi described — not merely someone who proclaims a distant future but someone who prepares the way of the one standing before them.

The parable of the children in the marketplace (vv. 31–35) is Jesus's sharp analysis of his generation's response to both John and himself. Children calling to their peers: “We played the flute and you did not dance; we sang a dirge and you did not weep.” John came fasting and ascetic, and they said he had a demon; Jesus comes eating and drinking, and they call him a glutton and a drunkard. No presentation satisfies those who have determined not to be satisfied. The person who has decided not to believe will find a reason to dismiss both the serious preacher and the joyful host. “Wisdom is justified by all her children” — the wisdom of God will be vindicated, not by the approval of the present generation, but by the fruit produced in those who actually receive it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A Pharisee named Simon invites Jesus to dinner — a gesture that is either genuine hospitality or a calculated opportunity for observation. The meal is interrupted by a woman “who was a sinner” — a phrase that, in first-century Jewish usage, likely means she was publicly known as a sexual sinner, perhaps a prostitute. She comes uninvited, stands behind Jesus (guests reclined at the table), weeps so copiously that her tears wet his feet, wipes them with her hair, kisses his feet, and anoints them with perfume. Every element of what she does is extravagant, uninhibited, and utterly unconcerned with the opinion of the dinner guests. She has something more important to express than social composure.

Simon's internal response is the response of careful religious propriety: “If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him, for she is a sinner.” His logic is: a real prophet would perceive her sinfulness and maintain appropriate distance from it. Jesus, perceiving Simon's thought (the prophet in front of him knows far more than Simon imagines), tells him a parable about two debtors — one forgiven a large debt, one a small one. Which loves more? Simon answers, correctly if reluctantly: “the one, I suppose, for whom he cancelled the more.” And then Jesus turns the parable into a mirror, held up to the dinner table: look at this woman. She gave me water for my feet; you did not. She kissed my feet from the moment I arrived; you did not greet me with a kiss. She has anointed my feet with ointment; you gave me no anointing. Her many sins are forgiven — as evidenced by the great love she is showing. He who is forgiven little, loves little.

The final declaration — “Your sins are forgiven... Your faith has saved you; go in peace” — is the chapter's answer to the question of what grace produces. The woman's extravagant love is not the price of her forgiveness; it is the consequence of it. She loves much because she has been forgiven much. And the faith that has saved her is the faith that drove her through Simon's door and to the feet of the one who could forgive. The Pharisees at the table respond exactly as they did in chapter 5: “Who is this, who even forgives sins?” They have been told who he is. They do not yet want to know.
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable of the two debtors is the theological key to the entire scene — and to the entire chapter. Forgiveness is the cause, love is the effect. This is the reversal of the moralistic reading that says “be more loving, and then God will forgive you more.” The gospel runs in the opposite direction: the more you understand what you have been forgiven, the more you will love. The woman's love is extravagant because her sense of her forgiven debt is accurate and large. Simon's love is small because his sense of his forgiven debt is small — or more precisely, because he does not yet believe he has a large debt. The Pharisee who considers himself basically righteous will never produce the love that flows from the woman who knows she is utterly lost and utterly forgiven.

The two Greek words for “forgiven” in this passage are significant: apheōntai (v. 47, “are forgiven”) is in the perfect passive tense — the sins have been forgiven and the forgiveness stands. It is not conditional on her continued performance of love. Her love is evidence of a forgiveness already accomplished; it is not the condition of a forgiveness yet to be granted. The direction of causation — forgiveness produces love — is the gospel's answer to every form of moralism that tries to produce love by moral effort without the prior gift of grace.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman who anoints Jesus's feet is the chapter's portrait of what it looks like to be genuinely overwhelmed by grace. She is not performing for the dinner guests; she is oblivious to them. She is not observing social conventions; she has left them behind. She is not managing her reputation; she has already forfeited it. What she is doing is the only thing she can do in the presence of the one who has forgiven her: giving everything she has — her tears, her hair, her perfume, her dignity — because the forgiveness she has received is worth more than all of it combined. The question the scene asks every reader is: do I feel forgiven like that?

Simon's failure is the failure of good morality without grace-shaped self-knowledge. He is not a bad man — he is a careful, observant, theologically serious man who has kept the law and maintained his reputation. What he has not seen is the size of his own debt. The person who does not see the depth of their own sin cannot be overwhelmed by the grace that forgives it, cannot produce the love that flows from that forgiveness, and cannot understand the woman weeping at Jesus's feet. The church that produces more Simons than sinful women has failed at the most basic level of gospel communication: it has not helped people understand what they have been forgiven.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a woman of the city, who was a sinner, when she learned that he was reclining at table in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster flask of ointment, and standing behind him at his feet, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head and kissed his feet and anointed them with the ointment... And he said to her, 'Your sins are forgiven... Your faith has saved you; go in peace.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The alabaster flask of ointment (alábastron myrou) would have been a sealed flask of expensive perfume — alabaster was used for luxury containers because it preserved the fragrance. The woman breaks or opens the flask — an irreversible act — and pours the entire contents on Jesus's feet. She gives all of it. The parallel scene in John 12 (Mary of Bethany) and the anointing in Mark 14 and Matthew 26 involve anointing of the head; Luke's version has the feet — the most humble posture of service. The woman does not anoint the head of a king; she anoints the feet of the one she has come to worship. The gesture is simultaneously the most humble and the most extravagant thing one could do.

“Your faith has saved you” (hē pistis sou sesōken se) is the formula of saving faith in Luke — the same words Jesus will say to the blind beggar in 18:42, and to the Samaritan leper in 17:19. The perfect tense of sesōken — “has saved” and continues to save — indicates not a momentary transaction but an ongoing state. The faith that drove the woman through Simon's door and to Jesus's feet is the faith that has brought her into a saved relationship. “Go in peace” — poreuou eis eirēnēn — is the Aaronic dismissal, the covenantal peace, the shalom that God gives to those who are right with him. She came in disorder and weeping; she leaves in peace.

8.title: The Word, the Storm, and the Power of the Kingdom
8.overview:
Chapter 8 is organised around the question of hearing and responding to the word — the parable of the sower, the lamp under a jar, and Jesus's redefinition of family as those who hear the word and do it all converge on the same theme before the chapter moves into four great demonstrations of kingdom power. After the teaching section, the chapter becomes a series of astonishing encounters: Jesus calms a storm on the Sea of Galilee, casts a legion of demons into a herd of pigs, heals a woman who has been bleeding for twelve years, and raises Jairus's daughter from the dead. The four miracle stories are not loosely connected anecdotes; they form a theological argument. Jesus has authority over the forces of nature, over the powers of darkness, over the long suffering of a diseased body, and over death itself. Nothing is outside the reach of his word.

The opening note about the women who accompanied Jesus and provided for the ministry out of their means (vv. 1–3) is characteristic Luke — he notices and names women at a point in history when their testimony was not counted and their presence was not recorded. Mary Magdalene, Joanna the wife of Chuza, Susanna, and many others: they are not background figures but named participants in the mission, financing the ministry that will change the world. Luke's Gospel is consistently attentive to those whom history overlooks.

The parable of the sower (vv. 4–15) is the parable about parables — the key to how the whole teaching ministry of Jesus works. The word is the seed; the hearts of the hearers are the soil; the response to the word determines everything. But the parable also functions as a warning and a comfort simultaneously: a warning that most hearers will not bear fruit, for a variety of reasons; a comfort that some will — “an hundredfold.” The harvest is certain; it comes to those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart and bear fruit with patience.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke records that Jesus travelled through cities and villages proclaiming the kingdom of God, accompanied not only by the twelve but by a group of women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities. The list is striking in its specificity: Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out; Joanna, the wife of Herod's household manager Chuza; Susanna; and many others. These women “provided for them out of their means” — they financed the Galilean ministry. The Greek word is diekōnoun, the same root as diakonos (deacon/servant) — they served the mission with their resources.

The significance of this brief passage is easily underestimated. In a culture where women were generally excluded from the public teaching and travel of a rabbi, Jesus's entourage included women as named, active participants. Mary Magdalene will be the first witness of the resurrection (24:10); Joanna is named again at the empty tomb. The women who provided for the ministry in Galilee are the same women who will be present at the cross (23:49) and the empty tomb (24:1–11). They are not peripheral; they are among the most faithful witnesses in the whole narrative. Luke sees them and names them when the other accounts would have left them anonymous.
verseByVerse.theology: The inclusion of women in the travelling band around Jesus is a quiet revolution in the social world of first-century Judaism. Rabbis did not travel with female disciples; the association would have been scandalous. Jesus's practice reflects his consistent pattern of including those whom the religious establishment excluded — and it anticipates the full inclusion of women in the life of the new covenant community (Acts 2:17–18; Galatians 3:28). The kingdom of God does not replicate the social hierarchies of the world it enters; it consistently subverts them in the direction of the image of God that every human person bears.
verseByVerse.examples: The women who supported Jesus's ministry “out of their means” are the model of financial stewardship in service of the gospel. They did not merely believe; they gave. The resources they had — probably income from estates or from their own trades — they placed in service of the ministry. The theology of giving that runs through Paul's letters (2 Corinthians 8–9; Philippians 4:14–19) has its roots in this practice: those who share in the blessings of the gospel are those who share their resources with those who carry it forward. The women of Luke 8:1–3 are the first and clearest expression of this pattern in the New Testament.

verseByVerse.quote: Soon afterward he went on through cities and villages, proclaiming and bringing the good news of the kingdom of God. And the twelve were with him, and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's household manager, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary Magdalene is the most prominent of the named women — and the most consistently misrepresented in Christian history. There is no basis in any of the four Gospels for identifying her with the sinful woman of 7:36–50 or with Mary of Bethany. Luke introduces her here with a single identifying detail: seven demons had been cast out of her. The number seven suggests completeness — she had been comprehensively in the grip of demonic power and had been comprehensively delivered. Her subsequent devotion to Jesus — present at the cross (23:49), at the burial (23:55), first at the empty tomb (24:1, 10) — is the devotion of someone who knows exactly what she has been rescued from.

Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod Antipas's household manager (epitropos — the steward who managed the estate), is significant evidence for the social reach of the Jesus movement. She was a woman of the Herodian court — the household of the man who had imprisoned and beheaded John the Baptist. That she and Chuza were somehow connected to Jesus's ministry suggests that the movement had penetrated even the household of its most dangerous political enemy. Grace reaches into the most hostile environments.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–15 — The Parable of the Sower and Its Explanation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The parable of the sower is Jesus's own explanation of why his ministry produces such varied responses — and why the disciples should not be surprised or discouraged by it. He tells the story publicly (vv. 4–8) and then explains it privately to the disciples (vv. 9–15), with an intervening comment about the purpose of parables. The story is simple: a sower scatters seed, and the seed falls on four different kinds of ground. On the path, the birds take it. On the rock, it sprouts but withers. Among thorns, it grows but is choked. In good soil, it grows and produces a hundredfold. “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

The disciples ask what the parable means, and Jesus's answer is one of the most important passages in all the Gospels on the purpose of parabolic teaching: “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that 'seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.'” This is an echo of Isaiah 6:9–10, the commission given to Isaiah after his vision of the seraphim — the hardening that results from persistent rejection of revelation. The parables are not simple stories designed to make things clear to everyone; they are an act of divine judgment on those who have already refused the light. Those who are open receive understanding; those who are closed find the parable becomes further opacity.

The explanation identifies the seed as the word of God and the four soils as four kinds of hearers. The path is the person who hears and the devil immediately takes the word away, lest they believe and be saved. The rock is the person who receives the word with joy but has no root — they believe for a while and fall away in a time of testing. The thorns are those who hear but are choked by cares and riches and pleasures of life. The good soil is those who hear the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience. The fourfold typology is not a rigid psychological classification; it is a searching mirror that each hearer is invited to hold up to themselves. Which soil am I?
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable of the sower is the foundational parable — Mark 4:13 records Jesus saying “Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables?” It establishes the principle that governs all the rest of Jesus's teaching: the response to the word determines everything. The word itself does not change; the seed is the same in all four soils. What varies is the condition of the heart that receives it. This is the basis of the New Testament's consistent call to prepare the heart — through humility, through the removal of competing loves, through the patient reception of the word — before the word can do its work.

The description of the good soil — “an honest and good heart” (kardia kalē kai agathē) — is the Greek ideal of the kalos kagathos, the beautiful and good person, applied to the inner life. But the content is entirely biblical: the honest and good heart is not the morally superior heart but the heart that is open, receptive, and fruitful — the heart that has been prepared by grace to receive grace. The “patience” (hypomonē) with which the good soil bears fruit is the patient endurance that the New Testament consistently associates with mature faith: not the impatient demand for immediate harvest but the willingness to tend the word and wait for God's timing.
verseByVerse.examples:
The parable of the sower is a diagnostic tool for self-examination. The question it asks every hearer is not “have you heard the gospel?” but “what has happened to the word in you?” Has it been snatched away before it could take root — by distraction, by the noise of competing messages, by the immediate interruption of the enemy? Has it produced initial enthusiasm that has not survived the first significant test? Has it been growing alongside competing loves — the love of money, the anxiety of life, the pleasures that crowd out the word? Or is it growing, quietly and with patience, toward a harvest?

The thorns — “cares and riches and pleasures of life” — are the most insidious of the four soils because they do not produce an obvious rejection of the word. The person choked by thorns is not an unbeliever in any obvious sense; they are someone in whom the word is growing alongside competing loves, and the competition is gradually winning. Jesus says the word is “choked” — strangled, cut off from light and nutrients. The diagnosis is not apostasy; it is suffocation. The remedy is not more effort but the deliberate removal of what is strangling the word — the act of dying to the competing loves so that the word has room to grow.

verseByVerse.quote: And when a great crowd was gathering and people from town after town came to him, he said in a parable: 'A sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it... And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold.' As he said these things, he called out, 'He who has ears to hear, let him hear.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Palestinian agricultural practice of scattering seed before ploughing (rather than after) explains why seed falls on what appears to be a path — the path may have been part of the field that would be ploughed later. The birds that snatch the path-seed are an image Jesus uses for the devil in the explanation (v. 12) — the enemy who moves immediately after the word is spoken to take it away. The speed of the snatching is the point: the word is most vulnerable in the moment immediately after it is heard, before it has had time to penetrate the surface of the heart. This is why sermons need to be prayed over, meditated on, and allowed to settle — the enemy is quickest in the moment of hearing.

“He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (v. 8) is not a redundant truism — everyone present has ears. It is a call to a different kind of hearing, a hearing that goes beyond the reception of sound to the reception of meaning, of intention, of personal address. The parable is not a puzzle to be solved intellectually; it is a word to be received personally, to be allowed to ask its diagnostic question of each specific hearer. The invitation to “hear” is the invitation to stop being a spectator of the story and to recognise that you are in it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — A Lamp Under a Jar and True Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two brief teachings follow the parable's explanation. The first is the lamp saying: “No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light.” The saying applies the parable's logic to the disciples: the word they have received is not private property to be kept; it is a lamp to be put on a stand so that others can see. The hiddenness that the parable warned about (the word snatched away, the word choked) is the enemy; the visibility and fruitfulness of the lamp on the stand is the goal. “For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor is anything secret that will not be known and come to light.” The word that is received will eventually be revealed by its fruit.

The second saying comes when Jesus's mother and brothers arrive wanting to see him, and he redefines family: “My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.” This is not a rejection of Mary or his brothers — Luke has already shown us the depth of the relationship between Mary and her son. It is a declaration that the primary identity of the community gathered around Jesus is not biological but covenantal: those who hear the word and do it. The hearing-and-doing of 6:46–49 (the two builders) now defines the family of God. This is the new covenant community — not a family by blood but a family by the word, held together not by DNA but by their shared response to the same Father's voice.
verseByVerse.theology: The lamp saying (v. 16) and the hearing-and-doing of the family redefinition (v. 21) are the application of the parable to the disciples' own vocation. They have been given the secrets of the kingdom (v. 10) — not for private illumination but for public proclamation. The word they have received is the lamp; the stand is the world they are being sent into. The parable of the sower describes what happens when the word meets different soils; the lamp saying describes what the disciples are to do with the word they have received — put it where others can see it.
verseByVerse.examples: The redefinition of family as those who “hear the word of God and do it” is the basis of the extraordinary community the church creates across every natural human division. People who share nothing by blood, culture, language, or class are family because they share the same word and the same response to it. This is the sociological miracle of the first-century church, which drew together Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free, men and women, into a community that the ancient world had no category for. It is the ongoing miracle of every church that takes the hearing-and-doing of the word as its defining identity rather than any natural affinity.

verseByVerse.quote: No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light... Then his mother and his brothers came to him, but they could not reach him because of the crowd. And he was told, 'Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, desiring to see you.' But he answered them, 'My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The warning of v. 18 — “Take care then how you hear, for to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he thinks that he has will be taken away” — is the principle of spiritual receptivity applied to hearing. The person who receives the word faithfully is given more; the person who hears without receiving finds that even the hearing diminishes over time. This is not an arbitrary divine allocation; it is the description of how the word works in those who are open versus those who are closed. Receptivity begets more receptivity; closure begets more closure. The capacity to hear is itself a gift that must be used or lost.

The timing of the family visit is significant: Mary and the brothers arrive during the public teaching ministry and cannot get through the crowd to reach Jesus. Luke does not tell us why they have come — Mark 3:21 suggests they were concerned he was “out of his mind.” Whatever their motivation, Jesus uses the moment to articulate the principle that governs all his relationships: the defining bond is not blood but obedience to the word of God. Mary herself, who “kept all these things in her heart,” is the model of the hearer-and-doer — which means she qualifies doubly as his family.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus and the disciples set out across the lake. Jesus falls asleep. A windstorm comes down on the lake — and these are fishermen, men who know this lake intimately, who have worked it in all weathers. When they wake Jesus with “Master, Master, we are perishing!” the fear in their voice is real: this is not an anxious overreaction; they are experienced mariners who know when a storm is going to kill them. Jesus “rebuked the wind and the raging waves” — the same language used for the exorcism of the demon in 4:35 — “and they ceased, and there was a calm.” And then he turns to the disciples: “Where is your faith?”

The disciples' question to each other — “Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?” — is the question the chapter has been building toward. The four miracle stories of chapter 8 each answer it from a different angle. He commands the wind and the water and they obey: this is the language of God's sovereignty over chaos in the Old Testament. In Psalm 107:28–29, the sailors in distress “cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress. He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed.” The disciples are living through the scene that Psalm 107 described — except that the one who stills the storm is asleep in the back of their boat. The Lord of the storm is asleep in the stern.

Jesus's sleeping in the storm is itself a theological image. He is not asleep because he is unconcerned; he sleeps because he is at peace. The one who says “do not be anxious” (12:22) practises what he preaches: there is no storm in the created order that can threaten the one who made it. His sleep is the sleep of perfect trust in the Father — the same trust he calls his disciples to embody. They wake him because they are perishing; he wakes because his disciples need him, not because the storm has threatened him. “Where is your faith?” — the question is not a rebuke for feeling fear, but an invitation to bring the fear to the one who is already in the boat with them.
verseByVerse.theology: The stilling of the storm is the New Testament's most direct claim that Jesus exercises the prerogatives of the Creator God over the natural world. In the Old Testament, only YHWH commands the winds and the sea: “He stilled the storm to a whisper; the waves of the sea were hushed” (Psalm 107:29); “You rule over the surging sea; when its waves mount up, you still them” (Psalm 89:9). The disciples' question “who then is this?” has only one answer: the one who rules the sea is present in their boat. The storm narrative is one of the most compact Christological proofs in the Synoptic tradition.
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples have Jesus in the boat and they are terrified. They have heard the sermon on the plain, they have seen the miracles, they have received the explanation of the parables — and when the storm comes, they are “afraid and marvelled” (v. 25). This is the honest portrait of early discipleship: knowing who Jesus is, in the abstract, is not the same as trusting him in the specific, embodied crisis of the storm. The passage is not primarily about the disciples' failure; it is about the Jesus who is in the boat with them. He does not abandon them in the storm; he stills it. And then he invites them to examine where their faith was during the storm — not to condemn but to grow.

verseByVerse.quote: One day he got into a boat with his disciples, and he said to them, 'Let us go across to the other side of the lake.' So they set out, and as they sailed he fell asleep. And a windstorm came down on the lake, and they were filling with water and were in danger. And they went and woke him, saying, 'Master, Master, we are perishing!' And he awoke and rebuked the wind and the raging waves, and they ceased, and there was a calm. He said to them, 'Where is your faith?' And they were afraid, and they marvelled, saying to one another, 'Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Sea of Galilee — 13 miles long, 8 miles wide, 680 feet below sea level — is notorious for sudden violent storms. The surrounding hills channel strong winds down onto the lake with little warning; the warm air rising from the surface clashes with the cold air descending from the surrounding heights. The disciples' alarm is professionally grounded: experienced fishermen know when a storm is fatal. The boat was “filling with water” (syneplērounto) — they were taking on water, sinking.

Jesus “rebuked” (epetimēsen) the wind and waves — the identical verb used in the exorcism of 4:35 and 4:41. The linguistic connection between exorcism and storm-stilling is a window into Luke's understanding of what is happening: the disorder of the natural world, like the disorder of the demonic world, is subject to the word of the Creator. The storm is not personified as a demon, but it is addressed as something that can be commanded — and it obeys. The created order, disordered by the fall, responds to the one in whom all things were created and by whom all things are held together (Colossians 1:16–17).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–39 — Jesus Heals a Man with a Demon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
On the other side of the lake — the Gerasene (Gentile) territory, east of the Jordan in the Decapolis — a man possessed by a legion of demons meets Jesus and falls at his feet. The description is harrowing: he wore no clothes, lived not in a house but among the tombs, had repeatedly broken the chains placed on him, was driven by the demons into desert places. He is a man who has been comprehensively dehumanised — stripped of clothing (the mark of dignity), of home (the mark of community), and of the capacity for self-determination (the mark of personhood). He is not a person; he is a site of demonic occupation.

The demons recognise Jesus immediately — “What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me.” The plural “legion” suggests an enormous number — a Roman legion numbered roughly six thousand soldiers. Whether the number is precise or hyperbolic, the point is the same: this man is under a massive, overwhelming demonic oppression. The demons beg Jesus not to cast them into the abyss (the place of their ultimate confinement) but to allow them to enter the herd of pigs on the hillside. Jesus permits this; the pigs rush down into the lake and drown; the herdsmen flee to report to the city. The local people come out and find the man “clothed and in his right mind” — sitting at Jesus's feet. And they are afraid.

The townspeople's response — they ask Jesus to leave — is one of the most telling details in the chapter. They have seen a man who was a terror to the community restored to sanity and dignity. They have lost a herd of pigs. And they want Jesus gone. The economic cost of the miracle, or perhaps the uncanny power that produced it, is more frightening to them than the man who was living among the tombs. The restored man himself wants to follow Jesus, but Jesus sends him home: “Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you.” He becomes the first missionary to the Gentile Decapolis — the witness sent not across the world but to the people who already know his story.
verseByVerse.theology:
The healing of the Gerasene demoniac is the most comprehensive exorcism narrative in the Gospels — and it is performed in Gentile territory, on a Gentile man, before an audience of Gentile pig-herders. The geography is the theology: the kingdom of God does not stop at the borders of Israel. The power over demonic oppression is not limited to the covenant people; it extends to every person who is under the dominion of the enemy, whatever their ethnicity or religious background. The Gerasene man is the Gentile counterpart to the Nazareth synagogue's demonised man (4:33) — both are liberated by the same word, with the same authority.

The man restored to his “right mind” (sōphrōn — the same word used for the sober-mindedness the New Testament calls for in leaders and in the Christian life generally) is sitting at Jesus's feet — the posture of the disciple (cf. Mary in 10:39; Paul at Gamaliel's feet, Acts 22:3). The demonic occupation has been replaced by the discipleship posture. This is the pattern of every genuine deliverance: the life that was dominated by the enemy is not merely emptied but reordered around Jesus. The sitting at the feet is not incidental; it is the theological point of the healing.
verseByVerse.examples:
The townspeople who ask Jesus to leave after seeing the man restored are the cautionary portrait of a community that values its economic security more than its neighbour's liberation. The pigs are gone; the man is well. The calculus should be straightforward. But the fear is real: something happened here that we do not control, and the loss of the pigs is tangible and immediate. The community that prioritises what it can calculate and control over what it cannot understand or manage will always find a reason to ask Jesus to leave. Every generation of the church has had to decide whether to welcome the disruptive grace of God or to manage it into something more comfortable.

The man's desire to follow Jesus — and Jesus's refusal, with the instruction to “declare how much God has done for you” — is the missionary call in its most particular form: go to the people who already know you. His witness among the ten cities of the Decapolis (Mark 5:20) plants seeds that will bear fruit when the early church moves into the Gentile world. The most powerful testimony is often not the stranger's proclamation but the neighbour's transformation. “Return to your home” is not a lesser commission; it is the first and most necessary mission.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they sailed to the country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee. When Jesus had stepped out on land, there met him a man from the city who had demons... When he saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before him and said with a loud voice, 'What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me.'... Then people went out to see what had happened, and they came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The name “Legion” the man gives in response to Jesus's question — “What is your name?” — is a Roman military term, adopted into Aramaic and Greek. In occupied Palestine, the word carried political resonance: the Roman legions were the visible symbol of occupation and oppression. The naming of the demons as “Legion” may carry an implicit political theology: the forces of spiritual oppression and the forces of political oppression share something in their character, even if they are not identical. Jesus defeats the Legion in Gentile territory — an anticipation of the gospel's eventual defeat of the Roman world's spiritual powers.

The pigs' rush into the lake and drowning has puzzled interpreters: why did Jesus permit the destruction of two thousand animals (Mark 5:13)? The most persuasive answer is that Jesus demonstrates the reality of the exorcism — the pigs' behaviour is the visible proof that something genuinely happened, that the demons are genuinely gone, that the man is genuinely free. The testimony of the herdsmen to the city and country (v. 34) is the report that brings the townspeople out to see the man restored. The loss of the pigs is the price of the evidence that changes the entire community's understanding of what has happened.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 40–56 — Jesus Heals a Woman and Raises Jairus's Daughter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The final section of the chapter is Luke's most carefully interlaced double narrative — the healing of the woman with the flow of blood woven inside the story of the raising of Jairus's daughter. Jairus is a ruler of the synagogue — a man of religious standing and social prominence. He falls at Jesus's feet and begs him to come to his house: his only daughter, twelve years old, is dying. Jesus begins to make his way there. The crowd presses around him. And a woman who has had a discharge of blood for twelve years reaches through the crowd and touches the fringe of his garment. Immediately her bleeding stops, and Jesus feels that power has gone from him.

The woman's story is the mirror image of Jairus's. She has suffered for twelve years — the same number as Jairus's daughter's age. She has spent everything she had on physicians; she is penniless, exhausted, ceremonially unclean, and has “no one” to advocate for her. Her approach is furtive — she touches from behind, hoping to remain anonymous in the crowd. When Jesus stops and asks who touched him, the disciples are incredulous (“Master, the crowd surrounds you and is pressing against you!”), but Jesus insists: he knows that power has gone from him. The woman, knowing she has been found out, falls before him trembling and declares before all the people why she touched him and how she was immediately healed. “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.” He does not rebuke her for the furtive touch; he names her — “daughter” — and sends her away healed and at peace.

While he is still speaking, word comes from Jairus's house: “Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.” The delay caused by the hemorrhaging woman has cost Jairus his daughter. Or so it appears. Jesus says: “Do not fear; only believe, and she will be well.” He comes to the house, sends away the professional mourners who are already weeping and wailing, enters with only Peter, James, John, and the parents. He takes the girl by the hand and says: “Child, arise.” Her spirit returns; she gets up immediately. He tells them to give her something to eat — the practical, physician's detail — and charges them to tell no one. The chapter ends with a resurrection and a meal, and the parents “were amazed.”
verseByVerse.theology:
The interlacing of the two stories is a masterpiece of narrative theology. The woman who is healed on the way to Jairus's daughter teaches Jairus — and the reader — that the delay caused by the woman's healing did not diminish Jesus's power or exhaust his compassion. The one who felt power go out of him for the woman has more than enough power for the dead girl. Jairus is being taught, through the woman's healing, to “only believe” — to resist the word that says “it is too late” and to trust the one who is walking beside him. The “too late” of the messengers is not too late for the Lord of life.

The woman's healing through touching “the fringe of his garment” (tou kraspedou tou himatiou autou) may refer to the tassels (tzitzit) Jewish men wore on the corners of their outer garments (Numbers 15:38–40; Deuteronomy 22:12) as a reminder of the commandments. Malachi 4:2 promised that “the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings” — the word “wings” (kanaphim) is the same word used for the corners of a garment. The woman who touches the fringe of Jesus's garment may be, knowingly or not, reaching for the healing in the wings of the sun of righteousness. The detail is medically specific (Luke the physician) and theologically resonant.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman's twelve years of suffering, her exhausted resources, her ritual uncleanness, her invisibility in the crowd — all of these are the conditions in which she finally comes to Jesus. She did not come while she had resources left; she comes when she has nothing. She does not come with a formal petition; she comes with a touch of desperate faith. Jesus's response — stopping in the middle of a crowd, insisting on finding her, naming her “daughter,” declaring her faith before everyone — is the public vindication of the person who came to him from the bottom of her resources. The crowd is not the obstacle to encountering Jesus; it is the context in which Jesus finds the one person who has come with nothing left to lose.

Jairus's journey — from the moment of his daughter's death-news to the moment of her raising — is the journey of faith pushed to its absolute limit. He has done everything he could: he found Jesus, he fell at his feet, he asked for his daughter's life. And then the delay, and then the word that it is too late. “Do not fear; only believe.” The faith Jesus calls for at the end of Jairus's rope is not the faith of a man who still has options; it is the faith of a man who has been stripped of every option except trusting the one who is walking with him. This is the faith that carries the weight of the resurrection — not the comfortable faith of the unchallenged, but the naked faith of the bereft.

verseByVerse.quote: And a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, who though she had spent all her living on physicians could not be healed by anyone, came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her discharge of blood ceased. And Jesus said, 'Who was it that touched me?'... And when the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling, and falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people why she had touched him, and how she had been immediately healed. And he said to her, 'Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The power that “went out from” Jesus (exelēlythuian dynamin — v. 46) is the only place in the Gospels where the healing power of Jesus is described as departing from him in this way. The detail is medically significant to Luke the physician: it suggests that the healing is not merely a divine fiat performed from a distance but a genuine personal expenditure — something of Jesus goes into the healing. This is consistent with the theology of 2 Corinthians 8:9 (“though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor”) and Hebrews 4:15 (he sympathises with our weaknesses): the Son of God's engagement with human suffering is not detached omnipotence but personal, costly, participatory power.

The title “daughter” (thygatēr) with which Jesus addresses the healed woman is used in this vocative form only twice in the Gospels — here and in Matthew 9:22. It is the most intimate term Jesus uses for a woman he has healed. Coming from the one who has just been called “Son of the Most High” by the demoniac, the address carries covenantal weight: she is a daughter of the kingdom, a daughter of Abraham (cf. 13:16 where Jesus uses the parallel “daughter of Abraham” for another healed woman), welcomed into the family of the Son of the Most High.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking, someone from the ruler's house came and said, 'Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.' But Jesus on hearing this answered him, 'Do not fear; only believe, and she will be well.'... But taking her by the hand he called, saying, 'Child, arise.' And her spirit returned, and she got up at once. And he directed that something should be given her to eat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Do not fear; only believe” (mē phobou, monon pisteue) is the most compressed summary of the call of Jesus in the Gospels: abandon the fear that says it is too late, abandon the calculation that says the situation is beyond hope, and entrust the impossible to the one who is walking beside you. The word “only” (monon) is the narrowing word: not fear and faith together; not faith alongside other strategies; faith alone. This is not the recklessness of someone who has not faced the evidence; it is the trust of someone who knows that the evidence that seems final is not final in the presence of the Son of God.

“Her spirit returned” (epestrepsen to pneuma autēs) — Luke the physician uses precise language. The girl was not in a coma (the professional mourners are already at the house — too quickly for a recent death to be uncertain); she was dead. Her spirit had departed, as it does at death (cf. Acts 7:59, where Stephen “gives up his spirit”). Jesus's command “Child, arise” — Talitha cumi in Mark's Aramaic — calls back what has departed. The instruction to give her something to eat is the physician's validation: she is genuinely alive, not in a trance; a revived person needs food. The practical detail is Luke's way of certifying the reality of the miracle.

9.title: The Turning Point: Cross, Glory, and the Road to Jerusalem
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is the pivot of Luke's Gospel — the hinge on which the whole narrative turns. Everything before it is the Galilean ministry of proclamation, healing, and gathering; everything after it (from 9:51 onward) is the great journey to Jerusalem, the road that leads to the cross. Within this single chapter, the Galilean ministry reaches its theological summit and its geographical end. The chapter contains the feeding of the five thousand, Peter's confession, the first and second passion predictions, the transfiguration, the healing of the epileptic boy, and the setting of the face toward Jerusalem. It is the most theologically dense chapter in Luke's Gospel.

The pivot on which chapter 9 turns is v. 51: “When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem.” The phrase “set his face” is the language of prophetic determination — Isaiah uses it of the Servant who “set his face like a flint” (Isaiah 50:7) in the face of suffering and shame. From this moment, every step Jesus takes in Luke is a step toward the cross. The transfiguration (vv. 28–36), which precedes this turning point, is the divine confirmation of the way that is being chosen — Moses and Elijah appear and speak of “his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.” The Greek word translated “departure” is exodos. The cross is not a defeat; it is the Exodus, the supreme act of divine liberation toward which all of Israel's history has been moving.

The chapter's central theological contribution is the collision between two kinds of glory. The crowds see a miracle-worker; Herod is perplexed by a rumoured prophet; the disciples feed five thousand from five loaves; Peter confesses the Christ of God — and immediately Jesus reframes everything. The Son of Man must suffer. Anyone who wants to follow must take up their cross daily. Whoever tries to save their life will lose it. The glory of the transfiguration is flanked on both sides by the shadow of the cross — and that is exactly the point. The glory and the cross are not opposites; they belong together. The cross is the path to the glory; the glory is the validation of the cross.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Twelve Sent Out; Herod's Perplexity
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus calls the twelve together and gives them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and sends them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal. The instructions are deliberately spartan: take nothing for the journey — no staff, no bag, no bread, no money, no extra tunic. They are to depend entirely on the hospitality of those they visit, staying in whatever house receives them and not moving between houses for better accommodation. Where they are not received, they are to shake the dust from their feet as a testimony against that place — the Jewish practice of shaking off Gentile dust when returning to the Holy Land, here applied to Jewish cities that reject the kingdom's messengers.

The sending of the twelve is the commissioning of Israel's representative leaders to extend the ministry of the kingdom beyond the reach of the one teacher and healer. The authority they receive is a delegated authority — the same authority Jesus has exercised, now given to them to exercise in his name. This is the pattern that will extend through Acts: the Spirit-empowered community carrying the same authority of the same word into the same world. The twelve are the first instance of the apostolic mission; Pentecost is its full inauguration.

Herod the tetrarch's perplexity — “John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things?” — is the question of a man who has killed the greatest prophet and is now hearing that something even greater than that prophet is happening. The three popular theories about Jesus (John raised from the dead; Elijah appeared; one of the old prophets risen) are all inadequate — and Herod knows it. “He sought to see him” — curiosity, not faith. He will see Jesus eventually, in 23:8–12, at the trial. It will not satisfy him. The question he asks here is the right question, but asking it without the humility to receive the answer is the condition that closes the door of grace.
verseByVerse.theology: The instructions to take nothing for the journey are not a practical travel policy but a theological statement about the nature of kingdom mission. The missionaries are not to carry resources that would make them independent of those they are sent to; they are to be entirely dependent on the hospitality of their hosts. This creates a bond of mutual vulnerability: the messenger depends on the receiver; the receiver depends on the message. The mission is not a delivery service where the messenger is self-sufficient; it is a relationship of shared need. The church that carries the gospel in the posture of self-sufficiency has lost something essential to the way Jesus designed the mission.
verseByVerse.examples: The shaking of the dust from their feet (v. 5) is the act that takes the refusal of a community seriously enough to mark it. The messenger who walks away from rejection without marking it has treated the rejection as inconsequential. The shaking of the dust says: what you have turned away from has eternal significance, and your turning away has eternal consequences. This is the missionary posture that neither abandons the rejected nor pretends the rejection doesn't matter — it bears witness to the reality of both the offer and its refusal, and moves on.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal... And he said to them, 'Take nothing for your journey, no staff, nor bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The pairing of “power and authority” (dynamin kai exousian) in v. 1 is significant: dynamis is the capacity to perform, the raw power; exousia is the right to perform, the delegated authority. Jesus gives the twelve both — not merely the ability to act but the right to act on his behalf. In a world ordered by patron-client relationships and chains of authority, the distinction matters: the twelve are not free-lancing healers using abilities of their own; they are accredited representatives exercising a granted authority. This is the structure of all Christian ministry: the ability comes from the Spirit; the right comes from the commission of the Lord.

Herod's three-theory typology about Jesus — John raised, Elijah appeared, an old prophet risen — reflects the categories available to first-century Jewish expectation. All three involve the return of someone from the past; none involves the arrival of someone genuinely new. The human mind defaults to known categories when it encounters the unprecedented. Jesus does not fit any of the three categories because he is not a resurgent prophet but the one toward whom all the prophets pointed. Herod's perplexity is the perplexity of someone who has all the right categories and none of the right posture for the one who exceeds them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Jesus Feeds the Five Thousand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The twelve return from their mission, and Jesus withdraws with them to the town of Bethsaida for rest and debrief. The crowds follow. Jesus receives them, speaks about the kingdom of God, and heals those who need healing. As the day declines, the disciples suggest sending the crowd away to find food and lodging — there are approximately five thousand men (plus women and children). Jesus's response turns the problem back to them: “You give them something to eat.” They have five loaves and two fish. Jesus takes them, looks up to heaven, blesses and breaks them, gives them to the disciples to distribute — and the crowd is fed, with twelve baskets of fragments left over.

The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle, besides the resurrection, recorded in all four Gospels — which signals its significance. The action is dense with typology: the five loaves and two fish in the hands of the Son of God feed a multitude in a desolate place, as the manna fed Israel in the wilderness. Moses interceded for bread from heaven; the one greater than Moses gives bread from his own hands. The twelve baskets of fragments (one for each tribe of Israel? one for each of the twelve disciples?) signal superabundance — the kingdom of God does not give minimum rations; it gives more than enough. The eucharistic language — took, blessed, broke, gave — anticipates the Last Supper and every celebration of the Lord's Supper since, where the same Lord takes what is offered, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to be distributed to his people.
verseByVerse.theology:
The feeding of the five thousand is the New Testament's great sign of the messianic banquet — the feast of the kingdom that Isaiah promised (Isaiah 25:6–9) and that the book of Revelation describes as the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9). Every time the church gathers at the Lord's table, it is participating in a foretaste of the final feast — the feast that the feeding in the wilderness points toward. The eucharistic action of Jesus (took, blessed, broke, gave) is the action that defines the church's life from its beginning: receiving grace, returning it in blessing, breaking it in service, giving it to the world.

“You give them something to eat” is one of the most demanding commands Jesus gives the disciples — not because the disciples can actually feed five thousand people from five loaves, but because the command is the invitation to bring what they have and trust him with the outcome. They bring the five loaves and two fish — everything they have, which is laughably inadequate — and Jesus multiplies it. The miracle happens not despite the disciples' involvement but through it. This is the New Testament pattern: bring what you have, however inadequate it feels; the one who multiplies is not you, but he works through your bringing.
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples' suggestion to “send the crowd away” is the reasonable, responsible, logistically sensible response to the situation. It is also the response that misses what Jesus is about to demonstrate. The disciples see a problem (hungry people, no food, late hour, remote location); Jesus sees an opportunity (the same hungry people, the same remote location, and the authority of the kingdom). Every pastoral and ministry crisis can be read through either lens: the lens that sees the limits of the available resources and suggests managed retreat, or the lens that sees the resources in the hands of the one who has already fed Israel in the wilderness. The disciples who suggest “send them away” are the same disciples who will distribute the bread. The command “You give them something to eat” transforms their perspective from the logistics of the problem to the resources of the kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: On their return the apostles told him all that they had done. And he took them and withdrew apart to a town called Bethsaida... Now the day began to wear away, and the twelve came and said to him, 'Send the crowd away to go into the surrounding villages and countryside to find lodging and get provisions, for we are here in a desolate place.' But he said to them, 'You give them something to eat.' They said, 'We have no more than five loaves and two fish — unless we are to go and buy food for all these people.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word “desolate place” (erēmos topos) deliberately echoes the wilderness of the Exodus — the same word used in the LXX for the desert where Israel wandered and where God provided manna. Luke is pointing his readers to the typological parallel: the God who fed Israel in the wilderness is present in the person who is about to feed the crowd in the desolate place beside Bethsaida. The parallel is reinforced by the action: Jesus has the crowd recline on the green grass (Mark 5:39 records this detail) in groups of fifty — an echo of the military organisation of Israel in the wilderness camp (Exodus 18:21, 25; Numbers 31:14).

The fourfold action — “he took the five loaves and the two fish, and looking up to heaven, he blessed them and broke them and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd” — is identical in structure and vocabulary to the Last Supper account in 22:19 (“he took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them”). This verbal parallel is deliberate and liturgically formative: the feeding of the five thousand is the foreshadowing of the Eucharist; the Eucharist is the ongoing participation in the abundance of the messianic feast. Every Lord's Supper is a remembrance of the Last Supper, which is a fulfilment of the feeding, which is a foretaste of the final feast.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — Peter's Confession and the Cost of Discipleship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus is praying alone, with the disciples nearby. He asks two questions. First: “Who do the crowds say that I am?” Answer: John the Baptist, Elijah, one of the old prophets risen. Second: “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answers: “The Christ of God.” And immediately, without celebration or expansion, Jesus charges them to tell no one — and begins to teach what “the Christ of God” actually means. “The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.” The Messiah must suffer. This is the interpretive revolution at the centre of the Gospel.

The passion prediction is followed immediately by the call to discipleship on the same terms: “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me.” The cross is not merely an event in Jesus's biography; it is the shape of the discipleship it requires. To follow a crucified Messiah is to follow in the pattern of crucifixion — the daily denial of the self that wants to save its own life, the daily taking up of the cross that looks like loss but is the path to the life that cannot be lost. “For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it.” The great paradox of the kingdom is stated as cleanly as it will ever be: the way to life passes through death; the path to glory passes through the cross.

The teaching concludes with a statement about the Son of Man's coming glory — “when he comes in his glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels” — and the enigmatic promise: “Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.” The most natural reading identifies this as the transfiguration, which follows immediately: a foretaste of the coming glory given to the three disciples who are present.
